instruction:
The reliability team retrains the kestrel model, which predicts pump failures from condition monitoring data. The last training data rebuild, run KP-23, computed wrong numbers, so the model cannot be retrained until the training data is rebuilt correctly as run KP-24. Nobody wrote down why KP-23 went wrong; the model team only noticed that its labels, its scaler statistics and its baseline scores did not hold up when they spot checked a handful of pumps against the plant records. Your job is to rebuild the data correctly and to leave behind a program the team can run again on the next estate.

Everything you have is in `/app/data` and `/app/docs`: condition telemetry exports from gateways and historians, asset, sensor and calibration records, controller alarms, work orders, failure notifications and their reviews, site rosters, weather observations, a run sheet, an errata register, two export profile registers and the governing standard `/app/data/fps4_rules.md`. The exact shape of every output is fixed by `/app/docs/output_contract.md`, and that contract is part of this brief.

The sources overlap and conflict, and some of them hold values that are wrong or superseded on purpose. Do not trust a file because it looks newer, cleaner or more complete, and do not reuse anything KP-23 produced beyond the one narrow use the standard allows. The standard, read together with the export profile registry and the errata register, decides every value; when a source and the standard disagree, the standard wins. Outputs are compared exactly: keys, columns, value types, decimal places, row order and empty values all count, so a figure that is close is still wrong. Where the contract asks for a fixed number of decimal places, write exactly that many.

## What to deliver

Write one program, `/app/out/build.py`, with three stages:

```
python3 /app/out/build.py phase1 DATA_DIR P1_DIR
python3 /app/out/build.py phase2 P1_DIR P2_DIR
python3 /app/out/build.py phase3 P1_DIR P2_DIR P3_DIR
```

Run it so that these 18 files exist:

- Phase 1, built from the input directory: `/app/out/p1/asset_registry.csv` (one row per asset), `/app/out/p1/sensor_daily.csv` (one row per asset day), `/app/out/p1/failure_events.csv` (one row per failure notification), `/app/out/p1/maintenance_log.csv` (services and oil samples), `/app/out/p1/site_days.csv` (one row per site day) and `/app/out/p1/run_parameters.json` (run settings and source attestation).
- Phase 2, built from the six phase 1 files and nothing else: `/app/out/p2/label_table.json`, `/app/out/p2/feature_matrix.json`, `/app/out/p2/scaler_stats.json`, `/app/out/p2/class_balance.json`, `/app/out/p2/quarantine_summary.json` and `/app/out/p2/bin_edges.json`.
- Phase 3, built from the six phase 1 and the six phase 2 files and nothing else: `/app/out/p3/train_ready.json`, `/app/out/p3/baseline_metrics.json`, `/app/out/p3/drift_report.json`, `/app/out/p3/site_allocation.json`, `/app/out/p3/amendment_impact.json` and `/app/out/p3/release_manifest.json`.

Fields, types, decimal places, ordering, encoding, line endings, the final newline and the empty value form of every file are in the output contract; follow it to the letter. The meaning of every field is in the standard.

Who uses what: the data scientists load `train_ready.json` straight into training and use `feature_matrix.json`, `scaler_stats.json`, `class_balance.json` and `bin_edges.json` to reproduce it; the release board reads `baseline_metrics.json`, `drift_report.json` and `site_allocation.json` before it signs off the retrain and assigns label reviews to the sites; the reliability engineers read `amendment_impact.json` to see how the decisions still pending after the freeze would move the labels; and the audit team compares `run_parameters.json` and `release_manifest.json` with the sources and with the files each phase handed on. The phase 1 tables are also used on their own by the site teams, so they must be right in their own terms and not only good enough for the later phases.

What each file is for:

- `asset_registry.csv`: the pump fleet as it stands at the freeze, which later phases use for holdout, commissioning and criticality.
- `sensor_daily.csv`: the calibrated daily condition values of each pump with its availability, alarm count and reading counts; every feature is built from it.
- `failure_events.csv`: the failure notifications with their review outcome, which decide the labels, and the decisions that were still pending at the freeze.
- `maintenance_log.csv`: the services and oil samples that feed the service and oil features and the maintenance exclusions.
- `site_days.csv`: whether each site was operating and how warm it was, which later phases need for exclusions and temperature rise.
- `run_parameters.json`: the effective run settings and one attestation row per source file, so the audit team can see what was read.
- `label_table.json` and `feature_matrix.json`: the samples that go into the retrain with their split, label and raw features.
- `scaler_stats.json`, `class_balance.json` and `bin_edges.json`: the statistics fitted on the training split.
- `quarantine_summary.json`: per site, how many readings were quarantined and why candidate samples were left out.
- `train_ready.json`: the standardised, weighted rows the training job reads.
- `baseline_metrics.json` and `drift_report.json`: how the fixed baseline score ranks failures and how far the test split drifts from training.
- `site_allocation.json`: how the label review budget is shared across sites under the caps.
- `amendment_impact.json`: the label changes the pending decisions would cause.
- `release_manifest.json`: the digests and row counts that tie the release to the files it came from.

You are done when all 18 files exist, each was written by the program from the directories named above, each stage also runs on its own into a fresh output directory, a second run gives the same bytes, and your final message lists what you wrote.

## Stage boundaries

Keep the work of each stage in that stage: phase 1 decodes and reconciles the sources into clean tables, phase 2 builds the samples, features and fitted statistics, and phase 3 builds the training rows and the reports. Each stage reads only the directories it is given and writes only into its own output directory, which it creates when it is missing. Phase 2 must work from any phase 1 directory and phase 3 from any phase 1 and phase 2 directories, including directories another run produced, so everything a later phase needs has to be carried by the earlier phase's files. No stage may look at directory names, at `/app/data` when it was not given it, or at any fixed location. Running a stage again on the same input must give the same bytes and must not break anything it wrote before.

The team will keep using the program after this run, which is why the three stages stay separate: when a new estate arrives they run phase 1 on it, check the phase 1 tables with the site teams, and only then run phases 2 and 3. A stage that quietly reaches back past its own inputs, or that only works on the files you can see today, is of no use to them.

The program is also run on unseen estates laid out like `/app/data`. They follow the same standard and the same output contract but carry other identifiers, values and export profiles, and every stage must be exact there as well. Wrong arguments and unreadable directories end with the exit codes and the one-line `error:` message the output contract describes.

## Environment

The machine has Python 3.12 with its standard library and PyYAML, and no network access. `/app/out` is yours to write; `/app/data` and `/app/docs` are read only in spirit even where the file system would let you write. The program may later be run by a different, unprivileged user, from a different working directory, with input and output directories in other places; it needs only read access to the directories it reads and write access to the directory it writes, and it must not rely on anything else you left lying around. A full phase 1 run on `/app/data` should finish well inside a few minutes on this machine; phases 2 and 3 are quicker. Large outputs are expected: the feature matrix and the training rows hold one row per kept sample.

## Requirements

Phase 1:

1. The phase 1 CSV files carry the contract headers, LF line endings and row order, and `run_parameters.json` uses the contract JSON layout.
2. `asset_registry.csv` gives each asset its site, model, OEM and serial as they stand at the freeze.
3. `asset_registry.csv` gives each asset its commissioned date, its decommission instant and its holdout flag.
4. `asset_registry.csv` gives each asset its criticality, setpoint and rated flow as they stand at the freeze.
5. `sensor_daily.csv` holds exactly the asset days the standard defines, each with its site.
6. Every asset day carries its availability.
7. Every asset day carries its daily vibration mean and maximum.
8. Every asset day carries its daily temperature.
9. Every asset day carries its daily pressure.
10. Every asset day carries its daily flow.
11. Every asset day carries its daily motor current.
12. Every asset day carries the setpoint and rated flow in force that day.
13. Every asset day carries its count of counted alarms.
14. Every asset day carries its usable and quarantined reading counts.
15. `failure_events.csv` lists exactly the failure notifications, each with its instant, failure day and status.
16. Every failure event carries its mode and its deciding instant.
17. Every failure event carries its pending decision, pending mode and pending instant columns.
18. `maintenance_log.csv` holds exactly the service rows.
19. `maintenance_log.csv` holds exactly the oil sample rows.
20. `site_days.csv` gives every site day its operating shift count and its operating flag.
21. `site_days.csv` gives every site day its ambient temperature.
22. `run_parameters.json` carries the run id, freeze, telemetry window, effective run parameters, holdout assets and site regions.
23. In `run_parameters.json` every in-scope source carries its role and its attestation digest.
24. Every reference copy carries its role and its attestation digest.
25. Every source carries its data record count.
26. On an unseen estate, phase 1 writes the exact asset registry, site days, failure events and maintenance log.
27. On an unseen estate, phase 1 writes the exact `sensor_daily.csv`.
28. On an unseen estate, phase 1 writes the exact `run_parameters.json`.
29. An unknown stage or a wrong number of directories makes the program exit with status 2, print one line starting with `error:` to standard error and write nothing.

Phase 2, for any phase 1 directory it is given:

30. It keeps exactly the samples the standard defines.
31. It labels every kept sample.
32. It gives every kept sample its split.
33. It writes the sensor window features of every kept sample.
34. It writes the service, age, oil and alarm features of every kept sample.
35. It writes the scaler statistics.
36. It writes the split counts and the class weights.
37. It writes the decile bin edges.
38. It writes the per-site quarantine and exclusion counts.
39. Every phase 2 file carries the upstream controls of the phase 1 directory it read.
40. Every phase 2 file carries the upstream digest of the phase 1 directory it read.
41. On an unseen phase 1 directory it writes the exact label table and feature matrix.
42. On an unseen phase 1 directory it writes the exact statistics files.
43. A missing or unreadable upstream directory makes it exit with status 3, print one line starting with `error:` and write nothing.
44. The delivered phase 2 files are exactly what the program writes from the delivered phase 1 files.

Phase 3, for any phase 1 and phase 2 directories it is given:

45. It writes the standardised feature values of every training, validation and test row.
46. It writes the sample weight of every row.
47. It writes the validation and test AUC of the baseline score with their row and positive counts.
48. It picks the validation threshold and reports its F1.
49. It writes the test confusion counts, precision, recall and F1 at that threshold.
50. It writes the drift report.
51. It writes the review budget allocation.
52. It lists exactly the label changes that the pending amendments cause.
53. It writes the count of events with a pending amendment and the label flips per split.
54. It writes the release manifest.
55. Every phase 3 file carries the upstream controls of the twelve files it read.
56. Every phase 3 file carries the upstream digest of the twelve files it read.
57. On unseen upstream directories it writes the exact training rows.
58. On unseen upstream directories it writes the exact report files.
59. The delivered phase 3 files are exactly what the program writes from the delivered phase 1 and phase 2 files.
60. Every phase 2 and phase 3 file uses the contract JSON layout.

Rules for the program:

61. Every result comes from the directories given: nothing in the program depends on the identifiers or values of `/app/data`.
62. Its output does not depend on the name or location of the directories it is given.
63. Phase 1 reads only DATA_DIR, uses only the Python standard library and the packages already installed here (PyYAML is available), and works offline.
64. Two runs on the same input give byte-identical files.
65. Phase 2 and phase 3 never read the input estate, only the upstream directories they are given.
66. Phase 2 and phase 3 results follow from the upstream directories given; they never read a fixed location such as `/app/out`.
67. The upstream digest a phase 2 or phase 3 file states is the digest of the upstream files that phase actually read.
68. The program never changes anything inside a directory it reads.

How to work:

69. Read `/app/data/fps4_rules.md` before you write `/app/out/build.py`.
70. Read `/app/docs/output_contract.md` before you write any phase 1 file.
71. Run `build.py phase1` on `/app/data` yourself and look at what it wrote before you finish.
72. Produce `/app/out/p2` by running phase 2 on `/app/out/p1`, and `/app/out/p3` by running phase 3 on `/app/out/p1` and `/app/out/p2`.
73. Before you rely on decoded figures, check the record count and control sum of each segment you decode against the control that segment publishes.
74. Keep the program readable: segment decoding, phase 1, phase 2 and phase 3 each sit in their own named functions.
75. End with a short message that lists the files you wrote under `/app/out` and any requirement you could not meet.
76. Stay inside the task: work only with `/app/data`, `/app/docs` and `/app/out`.
77. Do not claim a check passed unless you ran it and it passed.
78. Leave `/app/data` and `/app/docs` unchanged.
79. Do not install packages or reach the network.
80. Do not copy labels, splits or counts from the KP-23 export into your outputs.
81. Handle errors on purpose: no bare `except` and no `except` block that only passes.

instruction:
The files in `/app/data` hold one run of a clinical-assay quality-control recalibration: a stream of per-reading instrument signals for a small analyte panel, the reference tables, the governance inputs, and a complete written specification of how the reconciled recalibration report is worked out. The specification is split across the pipeline contract and the per-stage note files kept next to it in `/app/data`. The method coefficients and governance constants that the calculation depends on are kept in the recalibration spreadsheet and the governance document there, not in any plain-text file. Your job is to read the specification, work out which inputs feed which figure, and reconcile the run into the exact report it describes. Read the pipeline contract and the per-stage notes before you start writing the program. Every figure can be derived from the shipped files, and the work is to derive each one rather than copy it out of any single file.

Write one reusable program at `/app/out/derive_report.py` that reads a run in this layout from a data directory and writes the same reports into an output directory. It should run as `python3 /app/out/derive_report.py DATA_DIR OUT_DIR` and take both directories only from those two arguments, never from a fixed path. Then run it on the shipped run so that these files are written:

- `/app/out/summary.json`, the committed allocation summary
- `/app/out/policy_audit.json`, the reconciliation audit
- `/app/out/data_quality.json`, the objective and digest summary
- `/app/out/panel_analyte_glucose.json`, `/app/out/panel_analyte_calcium.json`, `/app/out/panel_analyte_lactate.json` and `/app/out/panel_analyte_creatinine.json`, the four per-analyte rollups
- `/app/out/matrix_rollup.json` and `/app/out/tier_rollup.json`, the matrix and tier rollups
- `/app/out/analyte_totals.json` and `/app/out/tier_analyte_membership.json`, the analyte totals and the tier membership map
- `/app/out/ordered_reading_index.json` and `/app/out/excluded_readings.json`, the ordered reading index and the excluded reading list
- `/app/out/analyte_committed.csv`, `/app/out/batch_committed.tsv` and `/app/out/matrix_weighted.psv`, the per-analyte totals, the per-batch totals and the per-tier weighted contributions
- `/app/out/carryover_ledger.xml`, `/app/out/objective_summary.yaml`, `/app/out/reconciliation_report.md` and `/app/out/run_status.txt`, the carryover ledger, the objective summary, the reconciliation narrative and the run status line
- `/app/out/provenance_manifest.json`, the provenance manifest

When you finish, state in your closing reply the objective value and the core sha256 digest your run produced, and the directory where you wrote the files.

Rules for the calculation:

- Take the recalibration coefficients only from the live sheet that the run profile selects, and take the five governance constants only from the governance document.
- Treat the files marked superseded as retired and derive nothing from them.
- Exclude the flagged quality-control readings before any ordering or aggregation happens.
- Apply the recalibration stages in the order the contract fixes. The committed per-analyte per-batch result is the base that every other figure is taken from, so one wrong reading of the ordering, the coefficients, the governance constants, the recovery floor, the batch cap, the convergence or the carryover pass shows up as many wrong figures at once.
- Apply the fixed-point rounding at each stage the specification names, not once at the end.
- Take the effective calibration lot as the smaller of the two declared lots.
- Apply the recovery floor before reweighting, and add the matrix shift after the floor clamp.
- Keep every recalibration figure as an exact integer or fixed-point value, because nothing is compared with a tolerance.
- Write every JSON file as compact JSON with sorted keys and a single trailing newline.
- Use only the Python standard library.

Your program will also be run on other runs in this same layout that you have not seen, built from the same rules, so it has to implement the specification in general and not depend on the shipped numbers. Only the paths listed above are collected.

You have 7200 seconds to complete this task. Do not cheat by using online solutions or hints specific to this task.

instruction:
A regional water and power utility has dumped one billing year of its meter
posting run into `/app/data` and then lost the program that read it. What
survives is the written contract at `/app/data/schema.md`, the four reading
files, the reference tables, and the policy file the utility posted against.
Your job is to rebuild the pipeline.

The contract is the authority on every rule: how a reading reaches its zone, its
currency, its rate and its billing cycle, which readings are malformed, how the
per account prepay wallet decides whether a reading posts at all, and the exact
shape of every figure you must emit. Read it together with the bytes. Deciding
which file feeds which figure is part of the work, so treat the directory as
something to explore rather than a list handed to you.

Deliver a reusable transform program at `/app/out/transform.py`. It takes an
input directory and an output directory and writes every artifact under the
output directory, so the same code posts a directory it has never seen. The
output directory it is handed may not exist yet, so create it when it is
missing:

```bash
python3 /app/out/transform.py <DATA_DIR> <OUT_DIR>
```

Use only the Python standard library; anything you pip install now will be
absent later. The program must not open network connections or start other
processes. Money is integer USD cents throughout, and every JSON artifact is
written with sorted keys.

Write the normalized reading stream to `/app/out/normalized.jsonl`, the book
wide roll-up to `/app/out/summary.json`, the data health report to
`/app/out/data_quality.json`, and the per tariff roll-up to
`/app/out/product_summary.json`. Write one file per top level zone at
`/app/out/region_central.json`, `/app/out/region_east.json`,
`/app/out/region_north.json`, `/app/out/region_south.json` and
`/app/out/region_west.json`, and one file per tariff class at
`/app/out/segment_consumer.json`, `/app/out/segment_corporate.json`,
`/app/out/segment_enterprise.json` and `/app/out/segment_smb.json`. The keys
inside each file are fixed by the contract. Every zone file and every class file
is written on every run, including a bucket that drew nothing.

Two warnings worth taking seriously. An artifact counts only when every single
value in it is exact, so one cent or one litre out of place costs the whole
file. And the figures interlock: an account's running wallet balance decides
which of its later readings are accepted, so a reading you post wrongly moves
the balance, changes which neighbours survive, and shifts every roll-up that
touches them.

Finish by posting a closing message that reports what you built, where each
artifact was written, and the nine closing report figures the contract defines.
Those nine appear in no artifact, so they have to come out of your own run.

You have 7200 seconds to complete this task. Do not cheat by using online
solutions or hints specific to this task.

instruction:
Our render track platform left a migration window in a state nobody trusts. The keyframe interval ledger under `/app/data/` is the only authority for the `interval_basis` value of each render track, and the generated interval snapshot, the interval index manifest, the encoder runtime state, the encode operations journal and the interval reconciliation report are all derived from it. The encoder runtime state disagrees with the generated interval snapshot for part of the fleet while the interval reconciliation report still reports agreement, so the surface meant to catch this says the system is fine. Work out what broke, decide which single authority record is wrong, and carry the platform through the whole recovery rather than patching the layer that shows the symptom.

Read everything under `/app/data/` before you commit to an account. The policy document there is binding and states the reference domain contract, the conversion of an alternate domain record, the settlement of a deferred lineage anchor, the state digest formula, the ordering and tie break rules, the recovery order and the preservation rules. Some evidence appears only once you have run part of the recovery, so expect to revise your account.

Write to `/app/out/data_quality.json` `root_cause` keyed `layer`, `entity`, `record_seq`, `field`, `recorded_reference_domain`, `required_reference_domain`, `recorded_value` and `canonical_value`, `rejected_hypothesis` keyed `name`, `layer`, `falsified_by_transition` and `falsifying_evidence` where the name reads `stale_index_generation`, `minimal_delta` keyed `authority_records_changed` and `changed_record_seq`, and `preserved_records` entries keyed `entity` and `reason` where the reason reads `later_amendment` or `retired_record_retained`, and, at the top level of the same file, `verdict` reading `in_sync` together with `authority_anchored`, `post_replay`, `layers_compared` listing every layer of the system in the order the operations catalogue records them, `mismatches`, `pre_repair_divergence_count` and `post_repair_divergence_count`. Write to `/app/out/normalized.jsonl` the durable state keyed `generation`, `authority_anchored` and `entries`, each entry keyed `entity`, `value`, `multiplier`, `lineage_anchor` and `state`, plus `record_type` reading `header` or `entry` per line on a `.jsonl` path. Write to `/app/out/product_summary.json` `digest`, `digest_modulus`, `pre_repair_digest`, `post_repair_digest` and `entity_metrics`, each entry keyed `entity`, `weighted` and `rank`, and `transition_order`, `dependency_order` and `revisited_repair` keyed `entity`, `transition`, `restored_lineage_anchor` and `superseded_lineage_anchor`, where `transition` names the recovery transition that rebuilds the layer holding the active lineage anchor, which you had to run a second time once the replay settled that anchor. Write to `/app/out/summary.json` `root_cause_entity`, `canonical_value`, `generation`, `digest`, `authority_records_changed`, `verdict` and `active_entity_count`. Write one partition view per label at `/app/out/region_central.json`, `/app/out/region_east.json`, `/app/out/region_north.json`, `/app/out/region_south.json`, `/app/out/region_west.json`, `/app/out/segment_consumer.json`, `/app/out/segment_corporate.json`, `/app/out/segment_enterprise.json`, `/app/out/segment_smb.json`, each keyed `partition`, `group` and `entities` with every entry keyed `entity` and `value` carrying the same value you wrote to the durable state, and ship the reproducer at `/app/out/transform.py`.

Every value, multiplier, weighted value, digest, generation and count you emit is an integer, so use no floating point and no rounding. Compute the state digest as the sum over active render tracks of the published value times the weighting multiplier, taken modulo 100003. Sort every entry list by render track name in ascending order. Assign rank by descending weighted value and break ties by ascending render track name. Give the dependency order as a topological order of the recorded edges with ascending render track name as the tie break. Exclude retired render tracks from the durable state and list them among the preserved records. Rewrite exactly one authority record and leave every other authority record at the value it already holds. Where two authority records amend the same render track inside a single generation, decide from the evidence which of the two the durable state carries, because their recorded order settles nothing. Write each JSON artifact as UTF-8 with two space indentation, line feed line endings and a trailing newline. Running your reproducer twice over the same input directory must produce byte identical output, and it must rebuild the durable state from the authority records, the replayed encode journal and the maps it reads rather than from any compiled, index or runtime layer. Confine `/app/out` to the artifacts named above.

The reproducer you ship must accept `--input` and `--out`, read only the directory given by `--input`, and write `reproduced_state.json` into the directory given by `--out` keyed `generation`, `digest`, `root_cause_entity`, `canonical_value` and `entries`, each entry keyed `entity`, `value`, `multiplier`, `weighted` and `rank`, with `rank` assigned by the same rule you use for the published metrics. It must use the Python standard library alone.

In your final message state the sequence number of the one authority record you rewrote together with the published value you settled for it, name the reference domain that record carried and the reference domain the contract requires and say why the recorded domain forces a conversion, list the recovery transitions in the order you ran them, report the state digest you reached, report how many render tracks diverged from the keyframe interval ledger before your repair and name them, and for each one name the derived layer that disagreed with the ledger and the value that layer carried, report the weighted contribution and the rank you recorded for the render track you repaired, name each record you preserved unchanged with the reason and the value it kept, report the count of authority records you changed, describe the reproducer you shipped, state which causal account you abandoned and which transition invalidated it, and explain how your final account covers both the evidence you had at the start and the evidence that appeared later. As you work, show the candidate reference rows you compared and the value each yields, and show the digest before and after the replay.

You have 7200 seconds to complete this task. Do not cheat by using online solutions or hints specific to this task.

instruction:
You are the confinement engineer on call for a vault estate whose privileged
administration binary runs under four independent enforcement layers. The
control plane that decides whether any given invocation is allowed to proceed
is called LGA. The engineer who was to write its solver left before starting
it, the estate has a backlog of recorded invocations nobody has checked, and
the change window cannot open until the solver exists and the grant plan it
emits has been produced.

Your job is to write that solver and to produce the plan it emits.

Everything the solver consumes sits under the directory `/app/data`. The
governing contract for the whole system is the file `/app/data/SPEC-LGA.md`,
and that file names five appendices and a glossary that sit beside it and are
part of the same contract. The specification is authoritative and complete. It
states every definition, every constant, every boundary, every encoding and
every output shape this task depends on. Where your instinct about Linux
confinement and that file disagree, the file wins, including where the rule it
states is not the rule a reasonable engineer would have chosen, and including
where it fixes the meaning of an ordinary word.

The corpus is flat and it is large. Nothing here tells you how many files there
are, what any one of them holds, or which encoding it uses. Working that out is
part of the task. Some files feed the decision and some carry material the
specification tells you to record rather than act on. A file being present is
not an argument that it feeds a particular output, and a field being present is
not an argument that it is trustworthy. The specification names the records
that are advisory and you are expected to notice them.

You have 7200 seconds to complete this task.

The work has two deliverables that stand or fall together. The first is the
plan itself, written as twenty-four artifacts. The second is the solver that
produced them, delivered as a source file so that it can be run again on a
corpus it has never seen. A plan that is correct but assembled by hand is not a
finished solver, and a solver that runs but emits a wrong plan is not a
finished plan. Both are graded.

The artifacts you write are exactly these, at exactly these paths:

```
/app/out/principal_registry.jsonl
/app/out/syscall_index.tsv
/app/out/pam_stack_resolved.csv
/app/out/selinux_type_graph.json
/app/out/seccomp_program.jsonl
/app/out/pam_verdicts.csv
/app/out/capability_ledger.csv
/app/out/domain_transitions.tsv
/app/out/seccomp_decisions.jsonl
/app/out/arch_dispatch.tsv
/app/out/admission_ledger.csv
/app/out/denial_attribution.jsonl
/app/out/blocked_syscalls.tsv
/app/out/capability_gaps.csv
/app/out/audit_continuity.jsonl
/app/out/relaxation_atoms.csv
/app/out/forbidden_atoms.tsv
/app/out/grant_plan.csv
/app/out/iteration_trace.jsonl
/app/out/minimality_witness.csv
/app/out/residual_denials.tsv
/app/out/conservation.json
/app/out/summary.json
/app/out/manifest.json
```

The solver itself is delivered as `/app/out/lgactl.py`, and it is the same
program, byte for byte, that wrote the twenty-four artifacts beside it.

The estate has recorded a population of runs. Each run is an ordered sequence
of events, and replaying one against the shipped policy either admits it or
refuses it. A run is admitted when no layer refuses any of its events. A run is
refused by the first event any layer refuses, and that one event fixes the
layer, the sequence and the rule the run is described by, whatever happens at
its later events. The four layers own different kinds of event and each has its
own algebra, and no two of those algebras resolve the same way. Getting one of
them right and the other three approximately right produces a population
verdict that looks plausible and is wrong.

Some of the recorded events are malformed. Every malformation that appears has
a stated repair, and a repair is a correction to apply rather than a reason to
drop a record. Repairs happen before a run is replayed, never during, and the
number of events each repair corrected is a figure you report at the end. An
architecture field left empty is not the same as an architecture field holding
a name, a capability written as a decimal index is the same capability as the
one written in full, and a permission field holding two names means the event
needs both of them.

Beside the policy the estate carries a catalogue of grant atoms. An atom is one
named, bounded relaxation, and each atom carries a cost. Some atoms are narrow
and name one object; others are broad and change a whole filter or a whole
stack line. Breadth and cost do not move together, and the cheapest atom that
touches the right object is frequently the wrong choice, because an atom that
would also let through a run the estate has marked as one that must stay
refused may never be used, however cheap it is and however well it would serve
the run in front of you. Deciding which atoms are ruled out that way is
something you do against the shipped policy, one atom at a time, and never
against a set of atoms taken together.

What you owe is the least set of permissible atoms that admits every run the
estate marked as one that must be admitted, while every run it marked as one
that must stay refused is still refused. Least here has a precise meaning the
specification fixes, and it is a property you have to demonstrate rather than
assert: for every atom your plan keeps, there is a run that your plan admits
and that the same plan without that one atom refuses, and you name that run,
the layer that then refuses it and the sequence at which it does. An atom with
no such run has no business in the plan.

Relaxing one layer does not finish a run. A run whose authentication was the
thing standing in its way can reach the executable label check and be refused
there instead, and a run whose label check clears can reach a capability it
does not hold. The plan therefore settles rather than being computed in one
pass, and it settles under a cap on how many passes it may take. A run that has
not been admitted when the cap is reached is recorded as such, with the status
the specification names for that case, rather than being quietly dropped from
the population or counted as satisfied.

Most of the artifacts describe the estate as it stands today, before any atom
is applied. A small number describe it after the plan is settled, and the
specification says which ones. One of them is the first artifact in the list
above, which carries for every principal the disposition its runs end in, and
that disposition cannot be known until the plan has settled. An artifact that
reports the wrong side of that line is wrong even when every number in it is
internally consistent.

Two of the artifacts are reconciliations rather than reports. One of them
closes the population over the whole run set and over the labelled part of it
separately, and the other summarises the shape of the work. Neither is derived
from the other, and copying a figure from one into the other rather than
deriving both from the run set is a way to produce two artifacts that agree and
are both wrong.

The audit trail matters on its own account. One capability in this estate is
advisory, meaning that a run missing it is not refused for missing it, and the
specification says how to tell which one that is rather than naming it here.
That capability is also what carries the audit trail, so a run that proceeds
without it proceeds with its audit continuity broken, and the artifact that
reports continuity distinguishes a run that lost the capability from a run that
held the capability and was refused the channel.

Output shape is part of the answer and not a matter of taste. Header rows are
written for some artifacts and suppressed for others, and the specification
says which. Columns appear in the order it states. Identifiers are emitted in
one canonical form and type names in a different one. A column the
specification declares is written on every row even when it is empty on most of
them. Every set is ordered by the key the specification states for it, which
is not always alphabetical. Mappings
emitted as JSON objects carry their keys in the order the specification lists
rather than sorted, numbers are emitted without a decimal point, a field
documented as a fixed-width code keeps its leading zeros, and files are written
as UTF-8 without a byte order mark and end with a newline. Two of the ordering
rules are stable sorts over keys that repeat across many rows, and one artifact
is ordered by a value that only a different artifact produces.

An atom names what it changes through a small structured target string, and one
of the elements that string can carry is commentary that changes nothing at
all. A solver that treats every element as meaningful will rule out atoms that
were never in question and will match atoms against refusals they have no
bearing on. The plan records, for each atom it keeps, the settling pass in
which that atom was first chosen, so an atom chosen early and kept through the
shrink carries the pass it was chosen in rather than the pass the plan
finished in.

One of the artifacts that reports what the shipped policy blocks is ordered by
a number that only the plan produces, so it cannot be written until the plan
has settled even though every other column in it describes the estate as it
stands today. Rows the plan never reached share a single value for that number
and fall back to the remaining ordering keys, so the ordering is total and two
correct solvers produce the same file.

The figures in your closing summary and the figures in your artifacts describe
one estate and must agree. A summary that reports a count the delivered ledger
contradicts is a summary of work that was not done, and the two reconciliation
artifacts exist so that an inconsistency upstream shows up as a number that
refuses to close rather than as a file that merely looks tidy.

Every artifact is written, including the ones that turn out to have nothing to
report. An artifact whose rows all vanished still carries its header line and
still ends with a newline (a JSON lines artifact with no rows is an empty
file), and an architecture that dispatched no event at all still carries its
row with zeros in every count. The catalogue artifact reports
every atom the estate carries, not only the ones the plan uses, so an atom that
repairs nothing and an atom that is ruled out both appear there with the
figures the specification asks for. The witness artifact carries exactly one
row for each atom the plan keeps and no rows for anything else, so its row
count and the plan's row count are the same number.

Runs the estate left unlabelled constrain nothing about the plan and are
reported exactly like the rest. They are replayed, they are attributed, they
are counted in the population totals and they appear in the ledgers. A solver
that filters the population down to the labelled part before it starts will
produce artifacts that are short by hundreds of rows and totals that no
reconciliation can close. The same goes for units, binaries and principals that
no run names: they exist in the corpus, they belong to no run, and nothing that
is keyed by run may invent a row for them.

The last artifact describes the other twenty-three as they were actually
written, giving for each of them the byte length, the count of newline
characters and the digest of its bytes, keyed by file name in the order the
specification lists them. It is written after the others and it describes them
rather than predicting them, so an artifact revised after the manifest was
built leaves the manifest wrong.

Nothing here tells you how many runs the estate recorded, how many atoms the
catalogue carries, how many of them are ruled out, how many passes the plan
takes to settle or how many runs end up recorded as not having settled. Every
one of those is something the corpus decides and your solver reports, and a
figure carried over from a guess rather than derived from the corpus will
disagree with the artifact that states it.

The solver you deliver is run as `lgactl.py CORPUS_DIR OUT_DIR`. It reads only
the corpus directory it is handed and writes only into the output directory it
is handed. It uses the Python standard library and nothing else, and it reaches
no network host at any point. Given one corpus it writes the same bytes every
time it runs. Given a corpus whose records are listed in a different order it
writes the same bytes, because every ordering the contract states is one the
solver imposes rather than one it inherits from whichever file a record
happened to land in. It exits zero when it has written every artifact, exits
two when it is called with the wrong number of arguments or handed a corpus
directory that is absent, and exits three when the corpus is there but a group
it needs is empty.

Leave `/app/data` exactly as you found it. Nothing under that directory is
yours to edit, rename, extend or delete, and a solver that rewrites its own
input is a solver nobody can re-run. Write nothing into `/app/out` beyond the
twenty-five files named above, so no scratch file, no intermediate dump and no
backup copy sits beside the deliverables when you finish.

Do not cheat by using online solutions or hints specific to this task.

When the work is done, finish with a short written summary. It confirms that
the twenty-five files were written under `/app/out`, naming `lgactl.py` among
them, it states that the solver used the standard library alone and reached
no network host, and it states each of the closing figures the specification
lists, by name and by value. Not one of them is a number you can copy out of
an artifact; each has to be worked out across the rows. They are the total
number of events the five repair rules corrected between them, counting an
event once for each rule that corrected it, the count of atoms that are not
ruled out and still repair no run that must be admitted, the mean cost of the
atoms in the plan rounded to two decimal places, and the count of principals
whose final disposition is that they were granted.

instruction:
Platform finance is closing October 2025 for the Kestrel monorepo CI fleets and needs the build-minute chargeback settled from the exports the fleets, the cache, the artifact store, the vendor and the ledger left behind. Everything you need is under `/app/data`: logs, registries, spreadsheets, databases, calendars, mail and the written policy documents. The sources overlap and disagree. Some of them are mirrors, drafts or working copies, some exported values are wrong or superseded by design, and several exports write the same kind of value in different conventions. The documents in `/app/data` define authority, scope, amendment, precedence and the conventions in force, and those written rules decide every conflict. `/app/data/settlement_authority.md` is the place to start.

## Deliverables

Write a reusable program and run it on `/app/data` so that these files exist:

- `/app/out/settle.py`: the program that produces every artifact below.
- `/app/out/attempts.jsonl`: one row per CI attempt with its settlement.
- `/app/out/lookups.jsonl`: one row per cache lookup with its outcome.
- `/app/out/targets.jsonl`: one row per build target with resolution, invalidation and ownership.
- `/app/out/actions.jsonl`: one row per cached action with hermeticity.
- `/app/out/artifacts.jsonl`: one row per stored artifact with its storage charge.
- `/app/out/invoice_reconciliation.jsonl`: one row per vendor invoice line with its reconciliation.
- `/app/out/team_chargeback.json`: charges per team.
- `/app/out/cost_center_ledger.json`: the ledger roll-forward per cost center.
- `/app/out/rate_resolution.json`: the rate windows in force per instance class and region.
- `/app/out/cache_effectiveness.json`: cache outcome counts per team.
- `/app/out/control_reconciliation.json`: every published block control with your recomputed figures.
- `/app/out/source_audit.json`: distinct record counts per input file.
- `/app/out/close_summary.json`: the close totals.

## Format

Every `.jsonl` artifact holds one compact JSON object per line. Money is an integer number of micro-dollars, durations are integer milliseconds unless the field name says seconds, instants are strings of the form `2025-10-03T04:05:06Z`, and a missing value is JSON `null`. Values are compared exactly at these units, including JSON types; key order inside an object does not matter.

## attempts.jsonl (row key `attempt_id`)

Each row has exactly the keys `attempt_id`, `job_id`, `attempt_no`, `fleet`, `runner`, `runner_rev`, `region`, `sku`, `instance_class`, `target`, `started_at`, `duration_ms`, `status`, `exclusion`, `billable_seconds`, `rate_micro_per_min`, `billing_class`, `reserved`, `cost_micro`, `owner_handle`, `team`, `cost_center`, and covers every attempt of the four fleets, including attempts outside the period.

1. `started_at` is the corrected start instant of the attempt.
2. `duration_ms` is the attempt duration as the documents define it.
3. `runner_rev`, `region`, `sku` and `instance_class` describe the runner revision in force at the corrected start.
4. `status` is the final status after errata that took effect.
5. `exclusion` is the documented exclusion reason that applies, or `null` for a billable attempt.
6. `billable_seconds` is the integer billable seconds, `0` for an excluded attempt.
7. `rate_micro_per_min` is the integer rate applicable to the attempt.
8. `billing_class` is the class the attempt bills under and `reserved` is a boolean telling whether a reservation applies.
9. `cost_micro` is the integer cost, `0` for an excluded attempt.
10. `owner_handle` is the handle charged for the attempt and `team` is that handle's team at the corrected start.
11. `cost_center` is the cost center charged at the corrected start.

## lookups.jsonl (row key `lookup_id`)

Keys: `lookup_id`, `attempt_id`, `action_key`, `shard`, `at`, `bytes`, `outcome`, `eviction_id`, one row per lookup in the three shard logs.

12. `outcome` is one of `hit`, `miss`, `stale_hit`, `evicted_hit`, `nonhermetic_hit`, `replay` under the cache rules.
13. `eviction_id` names the qualifying eviction for an `evicted_hit` and is `null` otherwise.

## targets.jsonl (row key `target`)

Keys: `target`, `kind`, `language`, `toolchain`, `constraint`, `version_at_open`, `version_at_close`, `invalidated`, `scope`, `owner_handle`, `team`.

14. `version_at_open` and `version_at_close` are the resolved toolchain versions at the period start and at its last second, `null` when nothing resolves.
15. `invalidated` is the boolean invalidation verdict for the target.
16. `owner_handle` is the owner from the ownership registry, `null` for an unowned target, and `team` is that owner's team at the period's last second.

## actions.jsonl (row key `action_key`)

Keys: `action_key`, `target`, `home_shard`, `hermetic`, `undeclared_inputs`, `input_bytes`, `disallowed_env`, `toolchain_version`.

17. `hermetic` is the boolean verdict, `undeclared_inputs` lists the undeclared input paths and `disallowed_env` lists the variables outside the allowed list, both sorted.
18. `toolchain_version` is the version named by the action's toolchain digest, or `null`.

## artifacts.jsonl (row key `artifact_id`)

Keys: `artifact_id`, `target`, `bytes`, `retained_seconds`, `storage_cost_micro`, `team`, `cost_center`.

19. `retained_seconds` counts retention inside the period only.
20. `storage_cost_micro` is the integer storage charge of the artifact.

## invoice_reconciliation.jsonl (row key `line_id`)

Keys: `line_id`, `runner`, `week`, `billed_micro`, `credit_micro`, `computed_micro`, `status`, where `week` is the 0-based position of the line's week in the period.

21. `status` is one of `closed`, `match`, `credited`, `mismatch` under the invoice rules.
22. `computed_micro` is the cost of the billable attempts the line covers.

## cost_center_ledger.json

An object keyed by cost center, each value with `opening_micro`, `postings_micro`, `charges_micro`, `closing_micro`, covering every cost center with an opening balance.

23. `postings_micro` sums only the postings that count for the period.
24. `closing_micro` is the closing balance of the cost center.

## Other aggregates

25. `rate_resolution.json` maps `"<instance_class>|<region>"` for every class and region in the rate card to a list of `[effective_instant, micro_per_min]` pairs: the row in force at the period start, dated at the period start, followed by each later row taking effect inside the period, in time order.
26. `control_reconciliation.json` maps every control id published in `/app/data/audit_annex.pdf`, plus the annex block figures published elsewhere, to `file`, `block`, `expected_records`, `expected_sum`, `records`, `sum` and `match`, where the last three are your recomputation and whether both figures agree.
27. `team_chargeback.json` maps every team that appears on an attempt or artifact to `attempts_billed`, `compute_micro`, `storage_micro`, `cache_credit_micro` and `net_micro`.
28. `cache_effectiveness.json` maps every team of a lookup's attempt to its count of each of the six outcomes plus `valid_hit_permille`, the integer floor of 1000 times hits over all lookups that are not replays, `0` when there are none.
29. `close_summary.json` holds `attempts_listed`, `attempts_billed`, `compute_micro`, `storage_micro`, `cache_credit_micro`, `net_micro`, `invoice_mismatches`, `controls_mismatched` and `closing_micro`, each summing or counting the matching artifact.
30. `source_audit.json` maps every input file name to `{"records": n}`, the number of distinct records in its primary table.
31. The artifacts use exactly the keys listed above, `.jsonl` rows sorted ascending by their row key compared as strings, UTF-8, LF line endings and a final newline.

## The program

32. `python3 /app/out/settle.py DATA_DIR OUT_DIR` reads only `DATA_DIR`, writes the thirteen data artifacts into `OUT_DIR`, creating it when needed, and exits 0. On a close of this size the program finishes within 15 minutes.
33. Run on a different close exported under the same documented layout, with fresh identifiers, values and convention placements, the program produces that close's correct attempt costs.
34. On such a close it produces the correct team and cost center of every attempt.
35. On such a close it produces the correct outcome and eviction of every lookup.
36. On such a close it produces the correct invalidation verdict of every target.
37. On such a close it produces the correct hermeticity and toolchain version of every action.
38. On such a close it produces the correct storage cost of every artifact.
39. On such a close it produces the correct status of every invoice line.
40. On such a close it produces the correct closing balance of every cost center.
41. On such a close it produces the correct rate windows.
42. On such a close it produces the correct control figures and verdicts.
43. Nothing in the program depends on identifiers or values of the shipped sample.
44. The output depends only on the contents of `DATA_DIR`, never on where that directory sits.
45. The program reads no input location other than the directory it was given.
46. Two runs on the same input produce byte-identical artifacts.
47. The program creates files only inside `OUT_DIR`.
48. The program leaves `DATA_DIR` unchanged.

## How to work

49. Before treating your decoding as final, reconcile it against the block control figures the documents publish.
50. Read every document that publishes field conventions before you write the decoders that depend on them.
51. Exercise your program on a copy of the corpus in another directory during the session and compare the artifacts with those of a run on `/app/data`.
52. When two sources disagree, settle it by the written precedence and amendment rules, never by which file looks newer or cleaner.
53. Keep reading, decoding, settlement rules and writing in separate functions of `settle.py` so each part can be checked alone.
54. Leave every file under `/app/data` unchanged.
55. Never copy a figure from a draft or mirror export into an artifact.
56. Your final message names each export you treated as a mirror, draft or working copy and the written rule behind each decision.
57. Work offline with Python 3 and its standard library only; nothing installed at run time is available later, and outputs go only under `/app/out`.

instruction:
A release train publishes a library whose exported scopes each carry an urgency rank. Every change to that surface is appended to the change ledger under `/app/data/`, and that ledger is the only authority on the platform. Three layers hang off it: a generated export snapshot that a compiler produces, a household index built from that snapshot, and a builder runtime that loads the index at startup. Downstream teams began reporting urgency ranks that disagree with what the recorders say they wrote, yet the surface meant to catch exactly this kind of drift reports that the platform is consistent. Work out what broke, decide which layer stopped agreeing with the ledger and why, and carry the platform through the whole recovery rather than repairing the layer that shows the symptom.

The evidence comes in several formats (CSV, pipe separated and newline delimited JSON shards, a SQLite database, an Excel workbook, Word addenda, YAML and JSON), and some files there are drafts, stale copies or superseded editions; the policy document's sources and precedence section says which file governs each input, and where an addendum amends the policy the addendum wins. Two parameters the replay depends on, the deprecation window and the urgency weights, are documented nowhere any more: recover them from the calibration controls exactly as the policy's parameter recovery section defines, including its rule for candidates that fit equally, and make the delivered reproducer recover them from whatever calibration evidence it is handed rather than carrying the values. The policy document there is binding and states the derived layers, the replay order, the record semantics, the inert reasons, the reference domain contract, the journal replay rules, the deprecation window and retirement order, the household version fold, the urgency totals, the surface digest formula, the control replay and the first divergent record, the divergence counts, the rank total order, the transition form, the revisited anchor form, the closed set of candidate causes with their falsifiers, the preservation rules and the serialization rules. Where this paragraph and the policy document differ in detail, the policy document governs.

Write `/app/out/scope_surface_core.json` with the keys `generation`, `release_version`, `active_scopes` and `retired_scopes`. Write `/app/out/reconciliation_summary.json` with the keys `authority_source`, `authority_ordering_key`, `control_ordering_key` and `effective_record_count`. Write `/app/out/urgency_metrics.json` with the keys `surface_digest` and `urgency_totals`. Write `/app/out/authority_verdict.json` with the keys `layers_compared`, `authority_anchored`, `pre_repair_divergence_count` and `post_repair_divergence_count`, where `layers_compared` lists every derived layer you weighed, in the order the policy document introduces them. Write `/app/out/resolution_trace.json` with the keys `transitions`, `revisited_anchors` and `inert_records`. Write `/app/out/root_cause_report.json` with the keys `root_cause`, `rejected_hypothesis` and `minimal_delta`, where `root_cause` carries `layer` and `observed_ordering_key`, `rejected_hypothesis` carries `name` and `falsified_by`, and `minimal_delta` lists one entry per scope whose urgency rank the generated snapshot got wrong, each entry carrying `scope`, `snapshot_value` and `authority_value`, ordered by scope name ascending. Write `/app/out/control_replay.json` with the keys `control_digest` and `first_divergent_seq`. Write `/app/out/rank_order.json` with the single key `rank_total_order`, holding the names of the scopes the recovered surface still exports, placed in the total order the policy document defines.

Work in integers throughout. There is no floating point anywhere in this task and no rounding. Serialize every JSON artifact as UTF-8 with two space indentation, line feed line endings and a trailing newline. Sort the keys of `active_scopes` and of `urgency_totals` by name ascending. Preserve the retirement order in `retired_scopes`. Treat everything under `/app/data/` as read only evidence. Where the ledger records two changes to one scope inside a window in which the recorded order and the effective order disagree, the policy document settles which one the durable surface carries, because the order the records arrived in settles nothing on its own. Running your recovery twice must produce byte identical artifacts, and deleting everything you wrote under `/app/out/` and running the recovery again must rebuild it from the ledger alone. Your output directory holds only the work this task asks for, so keep the names `sitecustomize.py`, `usercustomize.py`, `conftest.py`, `pytest.ini`, `json.py`, `hashlib.py` and `pathlib.py` out of `/app/out/`, because each shadows a standard library module a later Python process would load instead.

Deliver `/app/out/reproduce_scopes.py` as a standalone program that accepts `--input` naming a directory and `--out` naming a directory. It must read only the files inside the directory given to `--input`, it must import from the standard library alone, and it must write `reproduced_state.json` into the directory given to `--out` with the keys `surface_digest`, `generation`, `release_version`, `control_digest`, `active_scopes`, `retired_scopes`, `deprecation_window` and `urgency_weights` (an object keyed by class name), its `active_scopes` and `retired_scopes` carrying the same surface and retired list, in the same form, as `scope_surface_core.json`. The evidence it needs is the ledger shards under `ledger/`, `release_ops.sqlite`, `restricted_scope_map.xlsx`, every `policy_addendum_A<n>.docx`, `urgency_class_catalogue.json` and the `calibration/` directory, laid out under `--input` as they are under `/app/data/`. Anyone who hands it a directory holding the same evidence must get the same values back, and a directory holding a different ledger, journal, map or addendum must yield the values that evidence implies. Run it once against `/app/data/` with `/app/out` as its output directory, so `/app/out/reproduced_state.json` stands beside your work as a second derivation of the same numbers.

In your final message, name the standard library modules your delivered programs import, state which layer stopped agreeing with the ledger, name the candidate cause you eliminated and the observation that eliminated it, state which sources the shipped gate report places side by side, name the shipped narrative you set aside and the evidence that overruled it, and state a count of divergent scopes equal to the count you wrote into the authority verdict artifact and name those scopes. Also list every inert record by record sequence with the reason the policy assigns it, saying for any record whose inertness depends on the ordering what makes it inert under the authority ordering, state the surface generation together with the record sequence of the ledger record that sets it, state the household version you derived beside the version stamped on the generated snapshot, and state the anchor that settled each pending lineage anchor together with any journal operation you refused to follow while settling it. You have 7200 seconds to complete this task. Do not cheat by using online solutions or hints specific to this task.

instruction:
Implement the codec for SEALB, a proprietary opaque token container the KMS-9 envelope daemon writes. The container directory holds a written specification for the format together with supporting reference material; read the specification carefully and work out the grammar, the record modes, the state semantics, the rejection rules and the CRC trailer from what it documents. Everything a decoder and encoder need is written down somewhere under `/app/data`, and part of the task is deciding which of those files matters for a given question. Eight situations a container can present are settled by neither the specification nor its companion notes; deciding how the decoder treats them is part of the task.

Your job is to deliver a decoder and an encoder that agree with that specification on captures you will not see. Write the decoder to `/app/decode.py` and the encoder to `/app/encode.py`. `/app/decode.py`, invoked as `python3 /app/decode.py <input.nnc>`, should print one JSON object to stdout and exit 0, with nothing else on stdout, and it should still exit 0 when a file turns out to be damaged. `/app/encode.py`, invoked as `python3 /app/encode.py <document.json> <output.nnc>`, should read a document in that same JSON shape and write the container it came from, reproducing the original file byte for byte. A decoded capture looks like this:

```json
{
  "version": 1,
  "flags": {"reserved_bit_0": false},
  "record_count": 2,
  "base_value": 0,
  "records": [
    {"key": 1, "mode": "raw", "wide_value": true, "long_key": false, "raw_value": 42, "value": 42},
    {"key": 2, "mode": "raw", "wide_value": true, "long_key": false, "raw_value": -3, "value": -3}
  ]
}
```

The `records` array carries exactly `record_count` objects in file order. The `value` field is always the fully-resolved signed integer for that record, and the pre-resolution payload each mode records lets the encoder rebuild the file byte for byte. Keys are integers when short and UTF-8 strings when long. Every number must be an integer, and key order and whitespace inside the JSON are up to you. When a file has to be rejected, the decoder reports the failure as a single JSON error object carrying exactly the keys the specification defines for that error, following the precedence the specification sets out.

Alongside the two programs, leave a JSONL decoding of your own illustrative examples at `/app/out/decoded_examples.jsonl`, a deterministic summary of the grammar you recovered and the header layout and mode mapping at `/app/out/format_report.json`, a deterministic self-check that each illustrative example satisfies `encode(decode(bytes)) == bytes` at `/app/out/roundtrip_report.json`, and a deterministic summary of the documented error paths and their precedence at `/app/out/error_analysis.json`, each in the shape the decoder appendix lays out. Do not put hidden or reseeded corpus answers in any of these files; they cover only examples you construct yourself.

Both programs will be run against captures you have not seen, in a clean Python 3.12 that has only the standard library, so anything you pip install here will not be present at grading time. Only the six artifact paths named above are collected; `/app/decode.py` and `/app/encode.py` cannot import helper modules you write alongside them, and they cannot read `/app/data` while they run. SEALB is invented for this task, so there is nothing about it to find elsewhere. The program implementation must generalize: your decoder and encoder will be tested against captures in the same format on other domains, so your logic cannot memorize specifics of the shipped corpus, key on input filenames, reassign standard-library functions, or change its output between runs on the same input.

You have 7200 seconds to complete this task. Do not cheat by using online solutions or hints specific to this task.

instruction:
The files under `/app/data` are a telemetry corpus whose precomputed rollup is
numerically wrong. Recompute the rollup and deliver a fast standard-library
aggregator plus the reports it produces.

`/app/data/schema.md` is the authoritative specification for this corpus: where
any other file disagrees with it, the contract wins. It defines which inputs are
authoritative, how every figure is computed and rounded, and the shape of every
artifact. All arithmetic is exact, integer or exact-decimal, with no tolerances.

Deliver the optimizer at `/app/out/optimize.py`. It must expose
`aggregate(events_path, rules_path)` returning the result object the contract
defines and `resolve_rules(data_dir, scenario)` returning the resolved rules
object the contract defines, and it must also run as a script, `python3 /app/out/optimize.py
EVENTS_FILE RULES_JSON`, printing that same object to standard output as canonical
JSON with sorted keys and nothing else on standard output.

Write one scenario artifact per scenario at `/app/out/scenario_visible.json`,
`/app/out/scenario_peak.json`, `/app/out/scenario_steady.json`,
`/app/out/scenario_burst.json` and `/app/out/scenario_latency.json`, and write
the roll-up reports at `/app/out/perf_report.json`,
`/app/out/bottleneck_analysis.json`, `/app/out/recommendations.json` and
`/app/out/data_quality.json`. Every artifact must carry exactly the keys the
contract lists, must be serialised as JSON with its object keys sorted, and must
come out byte-identical when you run the same work again on the same data.

Your aggregator has to be measurably faster than the rescan baseline the contract
describes, compared as a ratio of repeated medians on one machine rather than as
an absolute time in seconds. The resolved threshold configuration carries the
relative ceiling your aggregator has to stay under, and
`/app/out/perf_report.json` has to report the ratio you actually measured on this
machine rather than a figure you assumed.

Use only the Python standard library. Do not install or import third-party
packages, and do not use the network at any point. Keep the aggregator reading
only from `/app`, the `events_path` and `rules_path` it is handed, and any
temporary scratch files it writes and reads back itself, and keep clock readings,
randomness and process-timing tricks out of the aggregator itself. Do not
hardcode a result that belongs to one particular input; apart from the fixed
strings the contract itself spells out, every figure a run reports has to come
out of the data that run resolved.

When you are done, close with a short written summary that names the files you
resolved as the authoritative inputs, says where you wrote the artifacts, and
states the corpus row, admitted, replayed and quarantined counts plus each
scenario's `event_count`, `checksum`, total `account_totals`, and total
`account_cost_cents` (the sums over accounts), exactly as your artifacts carry
them.

A result object looks like this in shape:

```json
{"label":"ROLLUP","window":[1000,9000],"event_count":2,"account_totals":{"A01":10},"region_totals":{"north":10},"kind_totals":{"alpha":10},"flag_counts":{"ok":2},"account_usage_wh":{"A01":30},"account_energy_kwh":{"A01":0},"account_cost_cents":{"A01":4},"top_accounts":[["A01",10]],"checksum":12345}
```

You have 7200 seconds to complete this task.
Do not cheat by using online solutions or hints specific to this task.

instruction:
The usage rating desk of a metered cloud service is replacing its slow aggregator, and nobody trusts the replacement yet. `/app/data` holds an extract from it: five scenario workloads, the rules file they are rated with, and the files that rules file names, including two closing journals of the retired legacy rating engine. The documents shipped with the data govern this work.

Write a fast, exact rating aggregator at `/app/out/optimize.py`. It must expose `aggregate(events_path, rules_path)`, returning the result object the documents define, and it must also run as `python3 /app/out/optimize.py EVENTS_CSV RULES_JSON`, printing that object on standard output as a single line: exactly the text Python's `json.dumps(value, sort_keys=True)` gives for it, followed by one newline (the reports below use a different layout). It will also be run on other extracts in the same layout, with their own file names, accounts, kinds, regions, flags, rate cards, journals and rules values, and it must give each of them its own correct result. The module reads only the workload and rules file it is given and the files that rules file names, and it creates, changes or deletes nothing. Its output must be byte-identical across runs, working directories, extract locations and output directories. With warmup calls and repeated timed calls, its median cost must stay at or below the relative target in the documents when compared with a re-walking implementation on the same input, and each call must finish within the time the documents allow. Keep timing code out of the module, which carries no clock and no randomness. Use only the Python standard library.

Then write the reports for the shipped extract: `/app/out/scenario_visible.json`, `/app/out/scenario_peak.json`, `/app/out/scenario_steady.json`, `/app/out/scenario_burst.json`, `/app/out/scenario_latency.json`, `/app/out/data_quality.json`, `/app/out/recommendations.json`, `/app/out/bottleneck_analysis.json` and `/app/out/perf_report.json`. Every report must match exactly, field for field and byte for byte. Leave the shipped extract under `/app/data` unchanged.

In your final message, answer each numbered question below on its own line. Each question describes a change to the shipped extract; everything else stays as shipped. Each changed extract is an extract in this layout in its own right, and the legacy engine's rules do not change.

1. What would the checksum of the visible scenario be if the rate card kept only the lines of batches RB01, RB02 and RB03, rate_figures.json listed only those three batches with their shipped figures, and every line of account M4415 in the standing journal recorded the standing `standard` instead of `premium`?
2. What would the checksum of the visible scenario be if the rate card kept only the lines of batch RB01, rate_figures.json listed only RB01, and the figure of RB01 were 15716 instead of 15766?
3. What is the largest whole-number `premium_floor` at which account C1788 holds premium standing in the burst scenario?
4. What would the total_score of the latency scenario be under the same rate card change as question 2 (only the lines of batch RB01 kept, with figure 15716)?
5. What would the checksum of the visible scenario be if the errata file ended with one more entry, `{"erratum": "ER-7", "booked_account": "C1648", "ts": 736, "field": "units", "value": "2"}`?
6. What would the total_score of the visible scenario be if row e548 of its workload had kind `stream` instead of `search`?
7. How many accounts of the visible scenario would hold a different premium standing from the one they hold as shipped if the governing registry record of account C1320 named C1694 as its sponsor?
8. What would the total_score of the latency scenario be if `carry_modulus` were 1034 instead of 997?

You have 7200 seconds to complete this task. Do not cheat by using online solutions or hints specific to this task.

instruction:
The quarter four settlement drop for the LedgerPort distribution network has
landed in `/app/data` as one flat directory of a hundred files. Finance needs
the quarter normalized and rolled up, and the drop is the only thing you get:
no upstream system is reachable and nothing in it is a clean export.

The written contract for the work is `/app/data/settlement_contract.md`. It
defines the canonical identifier form, the reference registries and how their
shards fit together, how to read each transaction feed, the ordered chain that
turns one raw row into one settlement record, the rejection code of every step,
how duplicates and reversals are resolved, and the exact field set of every
deliverable. Read it before you write any code. It names further files that
carry the pieces it does not restate, and those files name others. Which file
feeds which figure is part of the work, so treat the directory as something to
survey rather than a list handed to you. Several files look like the primary
input and are not, and several that look like noise hold a fact nothing else
carries. The drop also publishes its own declared counts and windows, so a
wrong reading of it can be caught before you ship.

Deliver a reusable program as one self-contained file at
`/app/out/transform.py`. It runs as a script
taking an input directory and an output directory, and it writes every
deliverable below under the output directory, so the same code gives correct
results for a drop it has never seen:

```bash
python3 /app/out/transform.py <DATA_DIR> <OUT_DIR>
```

It must work offline from the packages already installed in this image, must
read nothing outside the input directory it is given, must write nothing
outside the output directory it is given, and must produce byte-identical
output on repeated runs over the same input. Nothing in its logic may turn on
the particular identifiers, totals, file sizes or register values present in
this drop. A run has to finish within 1200 seconds on a drop the size of this
one, and within 300 seconds on a drop with a twenty-fifth of its rows. Do not
install anything while you work; use only what this image already has.

Run it once over `/app/data` into `/app/out`. The normalized ledger goes to
`/app/out/normalized.jsonl`, the quarter roll-up to `/app/out/summary.json`,
the data health report to `/app/out/data_quality.json` and the per-item
roll-up to `/app/out/product_summary.json`. Write one file per canonical
region at `/app/out/region_central.json`, `/app/out/region_east.json`,
`/app/out/region_north.json`, `/app/out/region_south.json` and
`/app/out/region_west.json`, and one per customer segment at
`/app/out/segment_consumer.json`, `/app/out/segment_corporate.json`,
`/app/out/segment_enterprise.json` and `/app/out/segment_smb.json`. Keep any
scratch files you make while exploring out of `/app/out`.

Every field name, value convention, ordering rule and rounding rule inside
those files is fixed by the contract and by the policy registers it points at.
Each one is compared field for field and type for type, so an integer field
carries an integer, a money field is a whole number of USD cents, and every
row of every output is checked rather than a sample. Write them
deterministically, with no timestamps, no durations and no run identifiers.

When you finish, report the accepted and rejected row counts your run
produced, name the policy registers your pipeline took its rules from, and say
which parts of the drop, if any, you could not interpret.

You have 14400 seconds to complete this task. Do not cheat by using online
solutions or hints specific to this task.
