instruction:
You are the storage engineer on call for a fleet whose application filesystem is
being relocated off an ageing source estate onto a tier of target devices. The
control plane that decides what the relocation still has to do is called STRATA.
The previous relocation run stopped part way through, and the fleet cannot
resume the move until a planner has been implemented and the plan it emits has
been produced. No starter planner is supplied.

Your job is to implement that planner and to produce the plan it emits.

Everything the planner consumes sits under the directory `/app/data`. The
governing contract for the whole system is the file `/app/data/SPEC-STRATA.md`.
That specification is authoritative and complete. It states every definition,
every constant, every boundary, every encoding and every output shape this task
depends on. Where your instinct about filesystems and that file disagree, the
file wins, including where the rule it states is not the rule a reasonable
engineer would have chosen. Read it in full before you decide what the corpus
holds, because the corpus does not announce itself and the directory listing is
not a description of the work.

The corpus is flat and it is large. Nothing here tells you how many files there
are, what any one of them holds, or which encoding it uses. Working that out is
part of the task. Some files feed the plan and some carry material the
specification tells you to record rather than act on. A file being present is
not an argument that it feeds a particular output, and a field being present is
not an argument that it is trustworthy. The specification names the values that
are advisory and you are expected to notice them.

You have 7200 seconds to complete this task.

The work has two deliverables that stand or fall together. The first is the plan
itself, written as twenty-four artifacts. The second is the planner that
produced them, delivered as a source file so that it can be run again on a
corpus it has never seen. A plan that is correct but assembled by hand is not a
finished planner, and a planner that runs but emits a wrong plan is not a
finished plan. Both are graded.

The artifacts you write are exactly these, at exactly these paths:

```
/app/out/object_inventory.jsonl
/app/out/device_topology.json
/app/out/extent_map.tsv
/app/out/symlink_topology.jsonl
/app/out/mutation_replay.jsonl
/app/out/scope_resolution.csv
/app/out/link_clusters.jsonl
/app/out/resume_state.jsonl
/app/out/xattr_ledger.csv
/app/out/special_nodes.tsv
/app/out/placement.csv
/app/out/sharing_expansion.jsonl
/app/out/allocation_projection.csv
/app/out/delta_workset.tsv
/app/out/metadata_workset.jsonl
/app/out/window_schedule.tsv
/app/out/split_ledger.jsonl
/app/out/descriptor_budget.csv
/app/out/cutover_sequence.txt
/app/out/rollback_plan.jsonl
/app/out/conservation.json
/app/out/cli_contract.json
/app/out/manifest.json
/app/out/summary.json
```

The planner is delivered as `/app/out/stratactl.py`. It takes the corpus
directory as its first argument and the output directory as its second, and it
writes those same twenty-four artifacts into whatever output directory it is
handed. It reads nothing outside the corpus directory it is given, it reaches no
network, and it imports nothing beyond the Python standard library. The rules it
applies are the ones you have read and built into it, so it does not read this
specification at run time and does not require that file to be present in the
corpus it is handed. Both directories reach it through those two arguments
alone, so its source carries no path from this machine anywhere in the code it
runs, not as a default, not as a fallback and not inside a message it prints. It is run
again on a corpus built from inputs you have never seen, exercising only rules
the specification documents, and the plan it produces there is expected to be as
correct as the one you deliver.

The specification fixes the exact column order, key order, sort order, encoding
and line ending of every artifact. Content that is right at the wrong path, or
right in the wrong order, or right with a column omitted, is a wrong artifact.
The order of keys inside a JSON object is the order the specification lists,
which is not alphabetical order, and an artifact whose keys have been sorted is
wrong. Every file is UTF-8 without a byte order mark, uses LF line endings, and
ends with exactly one newline.

Several definitions in that specification carry more weight than their length
suggests, and the plan is wrong in a way that is hard to see if any one of them
is read loosely.

The word relocatable has a precise meaning and it carries four conditions rather
than one. A status field alone does not settle it, the conditions are tested in
a stated order, and an object that fails more than one of them still reports
exactly the first that failed. Objects that are not relocatable still appear in
every artifact the specification fills with every object, and they take no part
in placement, sharing, scheduling or cutover.

Physical space and logical space are different quantities and the plan reports
both. A hole occupies logical space and no physical space, and copying one turns
a sparse file into a dense file and fills the target. A preallocated range
occupies physical space on the target and is never copied. A range that lives
inside the inode occupies neither and is never copied. Only one class of range
is ever read from the source at all, and the specification says which.

Ranges arrive with generations, they overlap each other, and they reach past the
end of the file they belong to. Each of those is a documented malformation with
a stated repair rather than a rejection, the repairs compose in a stated order
where more than one applies, and a range repaired into nothing has its own
stated outcome and is still reported. A range that has been repaired is used in
its repaired form everywhere afterwards.

Two paths that differ only in Unicode normalisation form are one path, and the
corpus carries both forms. An inode reached by several paths is one inode
holding one copy of its data, and the paths that are not its primary become
metadata operations rather than second copies. Which path is primary is settled
by a chain of four keys applied in order, and the corpus drives that chain to
every one of its four levels, so a chain that stops early gets the primary path,
or the level that settled it, wrong somewhere in the tree, and the artifacts that
order themselves by path follow a wrong primary there.

Symlinks are never followed for their contents. Their targets are preserved as
they are, relative and absolute alike, and the plan classifies each of them by
where it would resolve rather than by rewriting it. Resolution has a stated hop
cap, a stated outcome when the cap is reached and a separate stated outcome when
a chain returns somewhere it has already been, and both occur in the corpus.
Whether a symlink occupies any space at all turns on one boundary, and the
corpus carries targets sitting exactly on it and one byte either side.

Named pipes, sockets and device nodes are recreated from their metadata and are
never opened as though they held data. A device number is built from two fields
by a stated formula, one of those fields carries values the formula cannot hold,
and that overflow has a stated repair and is reported. An inode of one of those
kinds that carries no record of its own still reaches the plan.

The activity that happened after the previous run stopped is replayed against
what that run had already done. Whether an event is replayed at all is a
question about one boundary, and the corpus contains events sitting exactly on
it and one past it. An event that names something the inventory does not hold
has a stated outcome rather than being dropped silently. Replaying is what
decides which paths still exist, which inodes are still live, and which of the
ranges the previous run had already committed are no longer any use, and a
committed range is undone by a write that meets it or by a truncation that cuts
below it, where meeting and merely touching at an endpoint are different things.
What the previous run committed and what it merely started are also different
things. A missing checkpoint group is distinct from a group whose committed
value is `NIL`, and neither is numeric zero. The specification distinguishes
these cases from partial and excess commitments and states their outcomes.

Shared physical ranges survive as sharing only between devices that sit in one
share domain. Where the objects holding one shared range end up in more than one
domain, the range is materialised once per domain, and the extra copies are what
turn a comfortable target into a full one. Exactly one object owns each copy, by
a stated rule, and every other holder of that range becomes a metadata operation
rather than a copy, reporting the bytes the specification states for it.

Where an object lands is not settled in one pass. A device that cannot hold what
it has been given sheds work to another device, shedding changes which domains
hold a shared range, and changing that changes what every device is holding. The
attribution is rebuilt from scratch at the start of each round, while inside a
round what each device is holding moves as the work is shed, so the order the
devices are taken in is part of the rule rather than an implementation detail.
The specification states
how many rounds this runs for, how much each device sheds in one round, which
object it sheds and what happens to a device that is still overcommitted when
the rounds run out. The corpus reaches the last round.

The schedule is bounded twice over, once by the bytes a window will carry and
once by the number of inodes it will hold open at a time, and an inode already
open in a window costs nothing further. Whether a copy that does not fit is
moved to a later window or cut into pieces across several is not a judgement
call; the specification states which happens and when, and it states what
becomes of the bytes that never fit anywhere. Those bytes decide which objects
reach the cutover at all.

Cutover is ordered so that a directory precedes everything beneath it, and the
key that produces that order is not the key the plan already sorts by
everywhere else. Each cutover step carries the guard that has to hold before it
is safe and the action that undoes it, both chosen by stated rules from what the
rest of the plan says about that object, and an object the schedule could not
finish carries its own stated outcome instead of a step.

The identity that has to close is that everything a device has been given is
either copied in this run, resumed from what the previous run finished,
reserved without being copied, or left over. The residual is that total minus
those four, it is stated to be zero for every device, and it is zero only when
everything upstream of it is right.

Some rules of engagement apply to how you work rather than to what you compute.
The corpus under `/app/data` is read-only material and it arrives unmodified at
the end of the run, so nothing you do edits, moves, deletes or rewrites anything
inside it. `/app/out` is the complete, flat delivery root: it contains exactly
the twenty-five named regular files (the twenty-four artifacts listed above and
`stratactl.py`), with no extra entries, subdirectories or symlinks. No scratch
file, backup copy, intermediate dump or log is left there. Every figure you
report is one you computed from the corpus in this run rather than one you
assumed, and where you state a count it
agrees with the artifact it describes.

The plan has to account for the parts of the estate that are excluded as well as
the parts that move. An object that takes no part in the relocation is still
counted with its reason visible, a window that carries nothing still produces
its row, a device that receives nothing still produces its row, and an object
with no extended attributes at all still produces its row carrying zero and the
empty string. An artifact that silently drops the cases it decided were
uninteresting is a wrong artifact even when every row it kept is right. Where a
record has no value for an output text field, the field is present and carries
the empty string, and where it has no value for an output count, the field is
present and carries zero, except where the specification gives an explicit
sentinel such as the checkpoint committed value -1. These output conventions do
not change the input's `NIL`-only absence rule. A field is never omitted and a
row is never dropped to avoid stating an empty value.

The tables that report counts and the tables that report amounts have to agree
with each other. The bytes a device is said to hold are the bytes its objects
are attributed in another artifact, the bytes a window is said to carry are the
bytes the schedule placed in it, the number of objects a device holds is the
number of rows that name it, and the totals in the closure artifacts are the
totals of the tables they summarise. Producing each artifact independently and
never reconciling them is the failure this design is built to catch, because the
digests and the residual agree only when the whole plan agrees.

The closure artifacts carry a digest over an ordered list. The order is stated
and it is the order of the table the parts are drawn from, so a digest computed
over a sorted copy, or over a set, or over the parts in the order they happened
to be produced where the specification names a different order, is a wrong
digest even when every part is individually correct.

The planner decides what to do with malformed input rather than refusing it.
Every malformation the corpus carries has a stated repair, the repairs compose
in a stated order where more than one applies to a record, and a record that has
been repaired is used in its repaired form from that point on. A run that
rejects a malformed record, or that raises on it, or that repairs it for one
artifact and uses the raw form for another, produces a plan that disagrees with
itself.

The planner exits zero when it produces a plan. It exits with the usage code
when it is invoked with the wrong number of arguments, and with the policy code
when the path it was handed as a corpus fails to resolve to a directory. Those
two codes are stated in the specification and the contract artifact you deliver
reports them, so the numbers in that artifact and the behaviour of the planner
agree with each other.

Treat the run as one that has to be repeatable by somebody else. Running the
planner twice into two clean directories yields the same bytes both times, with
no timestamp, no host name, no absolute path of the machine it ran on, no random
identifier and no iteration order of a hash table leaking into any artifact.
Feeding it the same records in a different row order yields the same bytes as
well, because the ordering of every table is a property of the specification
rather than of the input.

Work only from the corpus and the specification beside it. Do not look up
solutions online. The domain is invented for this task, so an answer taken from
documentation elsewhere is an answer to a different question, and any figure
that came from a source other than the corpus in front of you is a fabricated
figure whatever it happens to match.

When the work is done, finish with a short written summary. Open it by naming
every one of the twenty-five files you delivered, each at its full absolute
path, so a reader can see the whole delivery without listing the directory.
Then state each of the following figures by name and value. The sum of the
utilisation figures in parts per million across every window row of the
descriptor budget. The number of window placements that opened a descriptor,
summed across every window. The total bytes the schedule placed across every
window. The total copy bytes across every row of the delta work set. The total
bytes recorded against the metadata operations. The total attributed bytes
across every device. The sum of the headroom across every device, which runs
negative where the tier is overcommitted. The inode on the five hundredth data
row of the window schedule in its canonical order. The total bytes the schedule
placed in window index zero across every device. The total bytes added across
the estate by sharing that spans more than one domain. The total bytes left
deferred across every device. The total length in UTF-8 bytes of every path in
the cutover sequence. The number of rollback rows that carry a step of zero. The
number of metadata operations whose verb is reflink. The number of objects shed
in the last shedding round. The number of devices that end overcommitted. The
number of shared physical ranges materialised into three or more copies. The
total bytes resumed from durable checkpoint entries across every device. The
number of hard link clusters whose primary path was settled at the fourth key.
The path on the first line of the cutover sequence.

instruction:
The files under `/app/data` are the complete export set and the written contract for a competitive arena game's quarterly ladder-season settlement. A prior settlement pipeline produced ladder ratings, rarity weights, calibrated smurf verdicts and credit payouts that did not tie out, and the settlement was rejected. Recompute the corrected settlement from these inputs and write the reconciled artifacts. This is a diagnosis-and-correction task, not a recovery or transcription task: the obvious reading of several stages is the wrong one, and correcting the faulty computation is the work. Filenames are deliberately generic, so read the contents to learn each file's role.

The stages interact: an early choice about which match attempts survive and which epoch anchors them changes the later unit, verdict, weighting, calibration, interval, and payout figures. Some load-bearing constants appear only inside a spreadsheet, a policy document, and a settlement addendum, and in no plain-text file, so those three must be read as carefully as the rest.

Here is what the corrected settlement owes, and you should read the full written contract under `/app/data` before you compute anything. Read the pipeline contract overview and every per-stage specification file, and apply the stages in the order the contract declares rather than the order the files happen to appear in. Build the economic match key from the documented identity fields rather than from any per-attempt identifier. Reduce the raw match attempts to one canonical row per match key using the documented seal and tie-break rules, and drop from the population entirely every match key that never sealed. Anchor each match on its first attempt and take the anchor epoch from that first attempt rather than from the canonical row.

Resolve each adjudicated verdict within the documented maturation window by revision-sequence order rather than by any wall-clock revision timestamp, and map verdicts through the documented crosswalk so that held and unmatured cases leave both the numerator and the denominator. Carry the documented cross-record running baseline per stratum in the documented order, so that no match resolves in isolation.

Convert every raw loot amount to integer ledger units using each currency's documented scale exponent, and obtain the count-to-ledger gain for raw ore from the live spreadsheet sheet only, leaving the superseded draft sheet and the superseded plain-text multipliers aside. Apply the latest season-patch drift reference dated on or before the anchor epoch. Use the frozen sampling stratum exactly as recorded, and keep the frozen stratum even where the current tier differs.

Compute the two-level rarity weights with the base rate and the nonresponse factor taken on their documented and different partitions. Apply the nonresponse inflation before quantization, then allocate each stratum's rounding residue exactly as the contract describes. Calibrate each score in log-odds space using the per-stratum parameters from the live workbook selected by the documented rule, and decide each match against its per-stratum threshold using the documented inclusive comparison.

Compute weighted precision, recall and F-beta, taking the overall figures as ratios of weighted totals and the macro figures as the documented weight-share-weighted means. Compute rewarded credits, forfeited credits, review cost and the pre-adjustment net using the definitions and the review unit cost that live only in the policy document. Apply the settlement levy and the settlement floor in the documented order, using the levy basis points and the floor that live only in the settlement addendum document and in no plain-text or spreadsheet file. Apportion the forfeited-credit basis-point shares so they sum to exactly the documented total using the documented tie-break. Compute the confidence intervals with the documented interval method on the documented effective sample size over the correct denominator subset.

Emit every artifact deterministically with the documented numeric types, including fixed-width decimal strings and integer counts or credits where the schema says so, sorted rows, line-feed endings and trailing newlines. Compute the manifest digest over the exact bytes of the four core files in the documented order. Also deliver the reusable standard-library program as `/app/out/settle.py`. It must accept exactly two positional arguments, `DATA_DIR` and `OUT_DIR`, read the complete contract and inputs from `DATA_DIR`, create the same twenty-nine settlement artifacts in `OUT_DIR`, and work for any valid corpus following the shipped contract rather than only the shipped rows. It must not read `/app/data` when a different `DATA_DIR` is passed. Write only the declared artifacts under `/app/out`; do not copy an input tree or a precomputed reference tree there. instruction:
# Chainfold run ledger repair

A sharded training run finished with bookkeeping nobody trusts. Twenty three log segments were uploaded by workers that reconnected at different times, so the segment files hold overlapping stretches of the run and three of them carry the earliest part of it. Two restarts resumed from checkpoints whose recorded cursors disagree with the stream. One shard changed hands while the run was live. Held out and duplicated examples were pulled from several shards after the manifests were cut, and nobody re-derived the step ledger afterwards.

The archive sits at `/app/data`. Explore it. Alongside the run material you will find the operator notes on record layout, ordering, precedence, arithmetic, validation, serialization and the output contract, plus a worked miniature run. Those notes are the specification. Every rule the task depends on is written there with examples. Read them before you build anything.

## What you must deliver

Write a run auditor to `/app/out/optimize.py`. It takes a data directory and an output directory, audits whatever conforming archive it is pointed at, and writes its reports into the output directory by base name. It reads nothing outside those two directories, needs no network and nothing beyond the Python standard library, and produces byte identical output every time it runs on the same archive.

Run it against `/app/data` with `/app/out` as the output directory so these land too:

- `/app/out/scenario_visible.json`, `/app/out/scenario_peak.json`, `/app/out/scenario_steady.json`, `/app/out/scenario_burst.json` and `/app/out/scenario_latency.json`, one per training profile
- `/app/out/perf_report.json` the cross profile summary with signed deltas against the baseline profile
- `/app/out/bottleneck_analysis.json` the ranked account of where records and examples leave the stream
- `/app/out/recommendations.json` the ordered remediation codes
- `/app/out/data_quality.json` the rejection, drift and reconciliation account

Every profile named in the archive gets its own scenario file, and every report carries the self describing fingerprint field the notes define.

## What the end state has to satisfy

The run is one ordered stream. File order, line order and file names carry no authority over it, and a segment uploaded late still belongs where its records say it belongs.

The optimizer step ledger is a running state. Each accumulation window closes against the width that is in force at the record being counted, and that width comes from the layered settings in the notes, resolved by the documented precedence and its named tie breaker. A restart boundary acts on whatever window is open when the stream reaches it, and the fate of that open window is itself a layered decision.

Work the restarts withdrew is withdrawn. Work a checkpoint never held was never held, whatever the recorded cursor says, and a cursor that disagrees with the reconstruction is an observation you must report rather than a number you may trust.

Every rejected, skipped and withdrawn record is counted once, attributed to exactly one documented reason resolved in the documented order, and the two reconciliation identities in the notes hold in every report at once.

All arithmetic is exact integer arithmetic under the named rounding rule, applied in the stated order. No floating point value may appear in any output. A zero denominator has a stated answer and a stated side effect, and both are the ones you must produce.

## Working conditions

You have 5400 seconds. Treat `/app/data` as read only and leave every file under it unchanged. Work only from the material under `/app/data` and your own reasoning; do not search online, do not fetch anything, and do not ask another person or service for the answer.

The run you can see is a quiet one. Rules that sit idle in it are live in other runs, and your auditor will be pointed at archives you have never seen, so build the policy rather than the answer. Hard coding values read off the visible run, branching on file names, or depending on anything outside the two directories will all come apart on another archive.

Leave `/app/out` holding only the ten deliverables above, each one complete, each one consistent with the others.

## Before you finish

Run the completed auditor twice against the same archive using two disposable output directories and compare every emitted file byte for byte. Remove those disposable directories, then make the required final run into `/app/out`.

In your final response, name all ten delivered paths, identify the archive evidence you used to reconstruct the optimizer step ledger, explain how the layered settings resolve the window width, and give the operator a short account of the run state and produced reports.

instruction:
A medical supply claims exchange has dumped one tariff year of its clearing
book into `/app/data` and then lost the program that read it. What survives is
the written contract at `/app/data/schema.md`, the four claim files, the
reference tables, and the policy file the exchange cleared against. Your job is
to rebuild the pipeline.

The contract is the authority on every rule: how a claim reaches its region,
its currency, its rate and its tariff period, which claims are malformed, how
the per member reserve ladder decides whether a claim is cleared at all, and
the exact shape of every figure you must emit. Read it together with the bytes.
Deciding which file feeds which figure is part of the work, so treat the
directory as something to explore rather than a list handed to you.

Deliver a reusable transform program at `/app/out/transform.py`. It takes an
input directory and an output directory and writes every artifact under the
output directory, so the same code clears a directory it has never seen:

```bash
python3 /app/out/transform.py <DATA_DIR> <OUT_DIR>
```

Use only the Python standard library; anything you pip install now will be
absent later. The program must not open network connections or start other
processes. Money is integer USD cents throughout, and every JSON artifact is
written with sorted keys.

Write the normalized claim stream to `/app/out/normalized.jsonl`, the book wide
roll-up to `/app/out/summary.json`, the data health report to
`/app/out/data_quality.json`, and the per item roll-up to
`/app/out/product_summary.json`. Write one file per top level region at
`/app/out/region_central.json`, `/app/out/region_east.json`,
`/app/out/region_north.json`, `/app/out/region_south.json` and
`/app/out/region_west.json`, and one file per segment at
`/app/out/segment_consumer.json`, `/app/out/segment_corporate.json`,
`/app/out/segment_enterprise.json` and `/app/out/segment_smb.json`. The keys
inside each file are fixed by the contract. Every region file and every segment
file is written on every run, including a bucket that drew nothing.

Two warnings worth taking seriously. An artifact counts only when every single
value in it is exact, so one cent or one unit out of place costs the whole file.
And the figures interlock: a member's running reserve decides which of its later
claims are cleared, so a claim you clear wrongly moves the reserve, changes
which neighbours survive, and shifts every roll-up that touches them.

Finish by posting a closing message that reports what you built, where each
artifact was written, and the nine closing report figures the contract defines.
Those nine appear in no artifact, so they have to come out of your own run.

solutions or hints specific to this task.

instruction:
You are the policy convergence engineer for the offline security policy compiler installed as sealb-ctl. The source archive `/app/data/tool.zip` ships a broken stdlib-only CLI. The written derivation contract lives in `/app/data/config_contract.md`, and `/app/data/config_schema.json`, `/app/data/defaults.json`, `/app/data/env_overrides.json`, `/app/data/validation_rules.json`, and `/app/data/change_journal.jsonl` complete the spine. The fifty evidence corpora `/app/data/c01_cve_severity.csv` through `/app/data/c50_oauth_scopes.bang` carry the rows. Every bit of every delivered artifact must be derived from these files; nothing may be invented, networked, or hand-written. Use only the Python standard library.

Satisfy every one of these requirements:

1. Extract `/app/data/tool.zip` safely to `/app/tool` and repair the broken CLI so every subcommand runs offline.
2. Replay `/app/data/change_journal.jsonl` strictly in ascending `seq` order; the file is intentionally out of order.
3. Classify each journal operation against `/app/data/validation_rules.json`; a `set` on an integer spine key must carry a JSON integer value inside its `bounds`, not a JSON string of digits.
4. Treat a valid `unset` as a restore to the `defaults.json` value for that key; last-set-wins while ignoring `unset` is wrong.
5. Generate the base spine as `/app/out/config.json` by driving the repaired CLI (init / set / validate), not by hand-writing JSON.
6. Produce the four zone profiles at `/app/out/profile_core.json`, `/app/out/profile_edge.json`, `/app/out/profile_dmz.json`, `/app/out/profile_mgmt.json` by starting from the finished spine, applying `/app/data/env_overrides.json` deltas, and replaying only that zone's valid journal operations.
7. Reduce the fifty corpora into `/app/out/aggregates.json`; the effective upper bound of every corpus is `hi + (R mod 97) + (J mod 31) + (E_i mod 7)` solved as a per-corpus fixpoint, where R is the finished-spine `rekey_interval_s`, J is the rejected-ops count, and E_i is the eligible-row count of corpus i under that same bound. The three shifts are co-prime (97, 31, 7), so a single misclassified journal op is observable in every one of the fifty aggregates.
8. Count a row only when its `zone` is byte-exactly one of `core`, `edge`, `dmz`, `mgmt`, its `flag` is byte-exactly `active`, and `str(int(value)) == value` on the raw field bytes. Reject `-0`, `-00`, `-000`, leading zeros, leading `+`, surrounding spaces, underscores, hex, floats, units, words, scientific notation, and every non-ASCII decimal digit (Devanagari U+0966..U+096F, Arabic-Indic U+0660..U+0669, Gujarati U+0AE6..U+0AEF, full-width U+FF10..U+FF19).
9. Mirror aggregates into `/app/out/aggregates.csv`, `/app/out/aggregates.tsv`, `/app/out/aggregates.xml`, `/app/out/aggregates.ini`, `/app/out/aggregates.env`, `/app/out/aggregates.md`, and `/app/out/aggregates.txt`, corpora in sorted name order; `.env` keys upper-cased.
10. Emit `/app/out/zone_totals.json` with the counted-row total per active zone across every corpus.
11. Emit `/app/out/corpus_index.json` with `count` and a `corpora` list carrying `name`, `format`, `op`, `lo`, `hi`, `eligible_rows`, and `value`.
12. Emit `/app/out/posture.json` with `aggregate_total`, `corpus_count`, `max_corpus`, `max_value` (ties broken by the earlier name), and `nonzero_corpora`.
13. Emit `/app/out/rejected_ops.json` with `rejected` (the ascending `seq` list of every invalid journal operation) and `count`.
14. Emit `/app/out/validation_report.json` with `ok` and `checks` covering `all_artifacts_present`, `config_matches_policy`, `config_scalar_flat`, `command_failures`, `rejected_ops`, per-zone `profiles` (`scalar_flat`, `trailer`), `corpus_count`, and `aggregate_total`.
15. Emit `/app/out/summary.json` with `tool`, `profile_tag`, `trailer`, `profiles`, `artifacts`, `artifact_count`, `inputs` (sorted names of every file under `/app/data`), `input_count`, `corpus_count`, and `aggregate_total`.
16. Emit `/app/out/report.json` through the repaired tool's `export-report` subcommand with `ok`, `tool`, `config_path`, `config_sha256` (sha256 hex of `/app/out/config.json` bytes), `trailer`, and `commands` (one object per CLI call, each with `argv`, `returncode`, `stdout`). No timestamps or run-dependent fields.
17. Rebuild the repaired tool deterministically as `/app/out/tool.zip` (ZIP_STORED, fixed epoch, fixed external_attr, sorted member order) so its sha256 is reproducible across runs.
18. Emit `/app/out/manifest.sha256`: one `<sha256>  <name>` line per delivered artifact except `report.json`, `tool.zip` and `manifest.sha256` itself, names in sorted order, two spaces between.
19. Every JSON artifact is written with these exact parameters: UTF-8, `json.dumps(obj, sort_keys=True, indent=2, separators=(",", ": "), ensure_ascii=False)`, plus a single trailing `\n`. Default `json.dumps(obj)` breaks the manifest.
20. The configuration must stay flat scalars only; no nested dicts or lists in `/app/out/config.json` or in any profile.
21. Keep the workflow deterministic and offline: no network, no wall-clock timestamps, no random seeds, no reliance on dict insertion order. Running the pipeline twice must produce byte-identical artifacts.

instruction:
You are the on-call operator for the Ironvault Bastion Control Plane at NONCE.
The security team shipped `nonce-ctl` (stdlib-only Python) with faults in
argument routing, key normalization, and derivation arithmetic. Repair the CLI
and use it to reconcile the Bastion policy end-to-end, then publish the full
artifact set to `/app/out/`.

The broken CLI archive is `/app/data/tool.zip`. The full input corpus (schema,
validation rules, environment overrides, sample profile hints, plus 50+ policy
files across CSV, TSV, JSON, JSONL, YAML, TOML, INI, .properties, .conf, .txt,
and PEM-style formats) lives under `/app/data/`. The load-bearing files feed
the derived scalar policy values: rotation cadences, MFA factor weights,
threat-actor tiers, cipher deprecations, trust-anchor scores, RBAC bindings,
firewall actions, hash-algorithm weights, attestation-signer status, egress
allow/deny lists, compliance framework weights, session lifetimes, and
audit-channel sampling deltas. Other files in the corpus provide security
domain context and are not required to be consumed by the derivation. The contract lives in
`/app/data/config_schema.json`, `/app/data/validation_rules.json`,
`/app/data/env_overrides.json`, and `/app/data/hardening_profiles.yaml`. The
`sample_config_*.json` files are hints only and must not be copied.

Start by extracting `/app/data/tool.zip` safely into `/app/tool`, rejecting any
archive member that uses an absolute path, a path-traversal segment, or a
symlink. Then bring the CLI up so `nonce-ctl` runs its full pipeline end to end
(`init`, `derive`, `set`, `validate`, `emit-profile`, `emit-artifact`,
`export-report`) and so a bare invocation without a subcommand exits non-zero
rather than silently defaulting. The `init` subcommand reads the schema at
`--schema` and emits a flat scalar configuration document with no nested
groupings. The `set` subcommand preserves keys exactly as passed and coerces
integer values including negatives. The `derive` subcommand computes every
derived security scalar from the corpus according to the interaction rules each
file declares through its own field values; no scalar may come from a sample
or a hard-coded constant. The `emit-profile` subcommand applies both the
`env_overrides.json` deltas and the matching offsets from
`hardening_profiles.yaml`. The `validate` subcommand enforces the numeric
bounds in `validation_rules.json` and the required keys in
`config_schema.json`, and rejects any nested value.

The main configuration at `/app/out/config.json` must be produced by running
the repaired CLI, not hand-written. It is a single flat JSON object of scalar
values, emitted with `sort_keys=True`, a two-space indent, and a trailing
newline. `/app/out/profile_dev.json` and `/app/out/profile_prod.json` come from
the same CLI via `emit-profile`; each carries every key of the main
configuration with its overrides applied, and its `trailer` value ends with
`:dev` or `:prod`.

`/app/out/report.json` records the CLI transcript. Its `commands` list holds at
minimum one `init`, one `derive`, one `validate`, two `emit-profile`, several
`emit-artifact`, and one `export-report`, each entry carrying `argv`,
`returncode`, and trimmed `stdout`. The `config_sha256` field equals the
sha256 of the delivered `/app/out/config.json` bytes and the `trailer` field
equals the config's `trailer`. The repaired CLI is repackaged as
`/app/out/tool.zip` so that unzipping it and running
`python3 cli.py validate --schema ... --config ... --rules ...` against the
delivered configuration succeeds.

The remaining artifacts follow directly from the reconciled corpus.
`/app/out/policy_matrix.csv` is the RBAC role x permission binary membership
matrix restricted to active roles as rows and active permissions as columns,
in ascending id order. `/app/out/rate_limits.tsv` has one row per non-deprecated
`internal` or `admin` endpoint, sorted by endpoint, with columns `endpoint`,
`zone`, `effective_rps`, `concurrency_delta`. `/app/out/rotation_schedule.yaml`
covers every secret class marked `required: true`, ordered by `class_id`.
`/app/out/mfa_quorum.toml` opens with the quorum threshold and lists one
`[[factor]]` block per enabled, non-deprecated, strong factor, sorted by
`factor_id`; the declared `quorum_threshold` equals both the factor-weight sum
and the main config's `mfa_quorum_threshold`. `/app/out/audit_sampling.ini` has
an `[audit]` section listing only channels for which
`sampling.<channel>.enabled=true`, with the channel's numeric `delta` as the
value.

Emit `/app/out/threat_scores.jsonl`, `/app/out/cipher_priority.txt`,
`/app/out/egress_allowlist.conf`, `/app/out/trust_anchor_manifest.pem`,
`/app/out/compliance_map.md`, and `/app/out/attestation_ledger.log` too. Each
contains only the active, allowed, or non-deprecated entries, ordered by id,
and stays consistent with the count-style scalars in the main config; for
example, the line count of `cipher_priority.txt` equals `active_cipher_count`.

`/app/out/session_policy.xml` is well-formed XML rooted at `<sessionPolicy>`
exposing `ttlSeconds`, `idleTimeoutSeconds`, `mfaQuorum`, and
`tokenEntropyBits` from the main config. `/app/out/derived_metrics.env` carries
one `IRONVAULT_<KEY>=<value>` line per derived numeric scalar, in the order
documented by `emit-artifact --kind derived_metrics`.
`/app/out/canary_thresholds.properties` is derived from the main config,
covering error percentage, latency budget, minimum signers, and maximum deny
rate. `/app/out/checksum_manifest.txt` carries one `<sha256>  <artifact>` line
per emitted artifact, matching the actual bytes on disk.

`/app/out/validation_report.json` is a JSON object with a top-level `ok`
boolean and a `checks` object. `checks` carries `all_artifacts_present` (true
when every declared artifact is present), `config_scalar_flat` (true when the
main config is flat and scalar only), `profiles_scalar_flat` (true when both
profiles are flat and scalar only), `command_failures` (the list of CLI
commands that exited non-zero, empty on a clean run), and `required_artifacts`
(the list of all 22 artifact file names). `ok` is true only when every boolean
check passed and `command_failures` is empty.

`/app/out/summary.json` is a JSON object with `artifact_count` (the number of
artifacts, 22), `artifacts` (the list of all 22 artifact file names), `inputs`
(the list of input file names under `/app/data`), `profiles` (exactly
`["dev", "prod"]`), `tool` (`"nonce-ctl"`), `format_tag` (`"NONCE"`), and
`trailer` (the main config's trailer).

The delivered artifacts must not contain any `http://` or `https://` URL, any
bearer token, or any `secret=`, `password=`, or `api_key=` fragment, and the
repaired CLI must not import `requests`, `urllib`, or `socket`. Use only the
Python standard library and the local files under `/app/data/`.

instruction:
A federated catalogue search broker ran a small program called the probe accounting engine. Every run it read the whole stream of metered partition lookups, resolved each lookup into a probe line, and then rolled the run up per partition and for the catalogue as a whole. When the broker controller was retired the engine went with it, and so did the per-lookup probe ledger for the last recorded run. What survives is that run's input and the two rollups the engine wrote for it, and all of it is in `/app/data`.

The written notes in `/app/data/broker.md` and `/app/data/reports.md` describe the shape of the engine and the shape of its three reports. They give the input columns, the ten pieces of carried index state, the fourteen stages in order, the status ladder, the key set of every report and the byte form each report is written in. What they do not give is any of the numbers. The gain and the governing count rule, the four keyed adjustment tables (the form of every entry as well as its figures, and how they round below zero), the credit release and its ceiling, the band edges, the two one-shot marks and what they do, the lock and its ratio, the size of the trailing record, the verb sets each rung of the ladder tests, the per-clearance tolerances, the whole debt subsystem, the figure a fetch adds to the baseline, the disposition thresholds, the counted status set, the order the partition rows run in and the two tie-breaks were firmware constants nobody wrote down. Those two notes bound what you are looking for.

The evidence you fit against is the run itself together with the two rollups the engine produced for it. The file `/app/data/lookups.jsonl` and the four tables beside it are the input, and `/app/data/ref_partitions.json` and `/app/data/ref_catalog.json` are what the engine wrote for exactly that input. There is no reference for the per-lookup probe ledger, so a wrong constant shows up only as a wrong total, count or disposition somewhere in those two rollups, and it will not tell you which lookup or which stage it came from. Neither rollup carries an index's debt or credit, so the debt subsystem has to be fitted through what it does to costs, statuses and dispositions. On top of that, no partition sits on more than one of the three plain keyed values at once, so no partition isolates a single adjustment and the constants have to be fitted together.

Rebuild the engine as a single reusable program at this path:

```text
/app/out/broker.py
```

The program takes two command-line arguments, the input directory first and the output directory second, and it writes `probes.jsonl`, `partitions.json` and `catalog.json` into the output directory in the exact form `/app/data/reports.md` describes, down to the key order, the row order, the separators and the trailing newline of every file. It has to work on any catalogue run in this schema rather than on the shipped one alone, because it will be driven over runs you have never seen, and the per-lookup ledger it writes on those runs is read as closely as the two rollups are. A run whose three files are not all byte-exact counts as wrong for that run. Use only the Python standard library. Work every figure out from the input files at run time and keep precomputed answers out of the program. Running it twice over the same input directory must write byte-identical files. Treat everything in `/app/data` as read-only input and leave it unchanged.

Check your fit rather than settling on the first reading that reproduces a few rollup rows. Set a block of the recorded run aside while you work the constants out, then replay that held-back block and check it too. For at least one constant on which two readings both fit what you have looked at, build a small input of your own on which they disagree and run both over it. Where two partitions share two of the three keyed columns and differ on the third, use that pair to narrow the adjustment on the column they differ on. Work at least one of the figures below out a second time through a calculation separate from the program you deliver. Before you finish, compare both of your own rollups against the two shipped reference files byte for byte.

Run your finished program over `/app/data` and give a closing report in your final message. State each of these twenty figures, using these names, as plain whole numbers measured over the shipped run, each of them a sum of the quantity named beside it, and keep every one of them out of the report files themselves:

```text
total_cost           cost over every lookup
ok_cost              cost over lookups resolving to ok
dropped_cost         cost over lookups resolving to dropped
setup_cost           cost over lookups resolving to setup
locked_cost          cost over lookups resolving to locked
heavy_band_cost      cost over lookups in the heavy band
warm_band_cost       cost over lookups in the warm band
light_band_cost      cost over lookups in the light band
fetch_cost           cost over lookups carrying the fetch verb
peak_phase_cost      cost over lookups in the peak phase
shoulder_phase_cost  cost over lookups in the shoulder phase
sparse_cost          cost over lookups on sparse charged partitions
stream_cost          cost over lookups on stream plan partitions
turbo_cost           cost over lookups on turbo pool partitions
cold_cost            cost over lookups on cold pool partitions
shared_index_cost    cost over lookups on partitions whose index another partition also names
derived_view_cost    cost over lookups on partitions whose index names a parent
replica3_cost        cost over lookups on replica 3 partitions
total_debt           debt_before over every lookup
flagged_debt         debt_before over lookups resolving to flagged
```

A partial engine that is written down and reported on is worth far more than a perfect one that never gets written, so put the program in place before refining the constants you are still unsure of. Once your last few attempts have taught you nothing new, state the twenty figures and end your turn.

The directory `/app/data` holds one billing period extract from a multi-region SQL query fleet, together with the documents that define how the fleet is metered and billed. The documents shipped with the data govern this work.

Deliver a program at `/app/out/transform.py` that meters an extract and writes its thirteen reports. It runs as `python3 /app/out/transform.py DATA_DIR OUT_DIR` and is self-contained: only it and its reports are collected from `/app/out`. Run it on the shipped extract, so that `/app/out` holds the program and its reports when you finish: `/app/out/normalized.jsonl`, `/app/out/summary.json`, `/app/out/data_quality.json`, `/app/out/product_summary.json`, `/app/out/region_central.json`, `/app/out/region_east.json`, `/app/out/region_north.json`, `/app/out/region_south.json`, `/app/out/region_west.json`, `/app/out/segment_consumer.json`, `/app/out/segment_corporate.json`, `/app/out/segment_enterprise.json` and `/app/out/segment_smb.json`.

It will also be run on other extracts in the same layout, so nothing in it may depend on this particular billing period. Each call finishes within 60 seconds. The program must leave DATA_DIR untouched, read nothing outside DATA_DIR and its own directory, and write nothing outside OUT_DIR. Its reports must be byte-identical across runs, working directories, extract locations and output directories. Every report must match exactly, byte for byte. Use only the Python standard library. Leave the shipped extract in `/app/data` unchanged.

Your final message answers the six questions below. Each what-if is worked out by rerunning the whole metering with exactly the change named, on a copy of the extract. Each changed extract is an extract in this layout in its own right.

1. In a copy where the row of query `q-2549985` in `queries.csv` has `duration_ms` 217843 and the row of query `q-0386103` has `duration_ms` 285337, what are the `charge_micros` of `q-2549985`, `q-0386103` and `q-1485251`?

2. In a copy where the row of query `q-6138339` in `queries.csv` has `duration_ms` 121209 and `scanned_bytes` 55733911552, what are the `charge_micros` of `q-6138339` and of `q-2068952`?

3. Start from the copy of question 1 and append one line to `corrections.jsonl`: a `void` with `correction_id` `c-ffff0` and `recorded_at` `2026-02-10T00:00:00.000Z`, naming whichever of the three queries of question 1 has the largest `charge_micros` there. Which query is voided, what are the `charge_micros` of the other two, and what is their sum?

4. In a copy where `tenant_merges.csv` has one more row, absorbing `tn-77fb` into `tn-5fef` with `effective_at` `2026-02-04T00:00:00.000Z`, and where the row of query `q-1637487` in `queries.csv` has `duration_ms` 71874, what are the `free_bytes` and the `charge_micros` of `q-1637487`?

5. Start from the copy of question 4. For each whole number k from 1 to 60, set the `daily_free_bytes` of the latest `PL-STARTER` version in `plans.json` to k times 1073741824. For how many of these 60 values of k does `q-1637487` receive zero free bytes?

6. Start from the copy of question 1. Over the whole numbers k from 1 to 1024, with the `daily_free_bytes` of the latest `PL-BUSINESS` version in `plans.json` set to k times 1073741824, what is the smallest k at which `q-0386103` receives more than zero free bytes?

In the same message, state the number of reports your program writes for one extract, and for every check you ran on your program, the number of extracts it covered and the number of ledger lines it compared.

instruction:
The cache placement optimizer for our CDN edge fleet has been producing wrong plans. Nodes it showed as having spare disk have been filling up, the RAM pin lists it hands to the edge team do not match what the nodes can hold, and the shield and spill budgets it allocates do not add up. The capacity team wants the optimizer rebuilt from scratch so the plans can be trusted again. Your job is to write a new optimizer program and use it to produce the full set of planning outputs.

For each cache node the optimizer works out how much disk each content property takes at its peak, compares that with what the cache volume can hold, decides which hot generations to pin in RAM within the node's pin budget, shares each PoP's shield pool across its nodes, ranks nodes by how soon they fill up, and then projects what changes once the already-approved policy changes that land after the planning cut take effect, including how the PoP spill budgets and capacity tickets are handed out. The work is split into three stages so that each stage can be checked and rerun on its own.

Everything the optimizer needs is under `/app/data`: cache configuration, inventory and directory exports, disk audits, sweeper schedules, the change register and its board minutes, codec benchmarks, exporter counters from several collectors, and a few other operational files. These sources overlap and disagree with each other, and some of what is shipped there is stale, superseded, out of scope or simply wrong. The authority is `/app/data/edge_capacity_standard_r7.md`: where any file, any tool default or the earlier optimizer run disagrees with it, the standard wins. The exact shape of every output, and how the second and third phases are calculated, is fixed in `/app/data/OUTPUT_CONTRACT.md`. Treat both documents as part of this brief.

## What to deliver

One program and eighteen output files, all under `/app/out`:

- `/app/out/build.py`
- `/app/out/p1/nodes.csv`, `/app/out/p1/properties.csv`, `/app/out/p1/policies.csv`, `/app/out/p1/footprints.csv`, `/app/out/p1/pending.json`, `/app/out/p1/pops.json`
- `/app/out/p2/pop_rollup.csv`, `/app/out/p2/class_rollup.csv`, `/app/out/p2/shield_alloc.csv`, `/app/out/p2/pin_plan.csv`, `/app/out/p2/risk_rank.csv`, `/app/out/p2/manifest.json`
- `/app/out/p3/projection.csv`, `/app/out/p3/pop_outlook.csv`, `/app/out/p3/spill_alloc.csv`, `/app/out/p3/tickets.csv`, `/app/out/p3/class_drift.csv`, `/app/out/p3/manifest.json`

The program runs in three stages, exactly like this:

```
python3 /app/out/build.py phase1 <DATA_DIR> <P1_DIR>
python3 /app/out/build.py phase2 <P1_DIR> <P2_DIR>
python3 /app/out/build.py phase3 <P1_DIR> <P2_DIR> <P3_DIR>
```

Phase 1 works from the input directory. Phase 2 works from the six phase 1 files and nothing else. Phase 3 works from the six phase 1 files and the six phase 2 files and nothing else. The pending amendments that take effect after the planning cut are carried through phase 1 and phase 2 untouched and are applied only in phase 3. Each stage must create its output directory if it does not exist, must work on any directories it is handed (not just `/app/data` and `/app/out`), and must be reusable on fresh copies. Produce the eighteen files under `/app/out/p1`, `/app/out/p2` and `/app/out/p3` by running your program on `/app/data` in that order.

## What each artifact holds

- `/app/out/p1/nodes.csv`: one row per in-scope node with its PoP, class, tier, media, usable bytes, base usage, post-cut usage, reported prior peak, sweep interval and memory.
- `/app/out/p1/properties.csv`: one row per (node, property) pair with the production exporter instance, the number of kept readings and the daily volume in bytes.
- `/app/out/p1/policies.csv`: the same pairs with their versions, refresh, effective refresh, storage flags, codec and compression ratio.
- `/app/out/p1/footprints.csv`: the same pairs with cycle bytes and the hot, stale and peak footprint in KiB.
- `/app/out/p1/pending.json`: the planning cut and the approved amendments that take effect after it.
- `/app/out/p1/pops.json`: the prod PoPs with offset, shield pool, spill budget, ticket quota, RAM pin percentage, pin budget and in-scope node count.
- `/app/out/p2/pop_rollup.csv` and `/app/out/p2/class_rollup.csv`: per-PoP and per-class totals.
- `/app/out/p2/shield_alloc.csv` and `/app/out/p2/pin_plan.csv`: the shield pool allocation and the RAM pin plan.
- `/app/out/p2/risk_rank.csv`: headroom, days to full and rank per node.

The contract gives every column, its order and its exact rules. The conventions that apply everywhere:

- Files are UTF-8 with LF line endings, a final newline and no byte order mark.
- CSV files are comma separated with the contract's header line, no quoting and no padding. An empty field means null. Booleans are written `1` and `0`. Integers are plain base 10.
- Fields ending in `_bytes` are bytes, fields ending in `_kib` are KiB and fields ending in `_mib` are MiB. Ratios carry 2 decimals, densities and days 2 decimals and shares 4 decimals, all rounded half to even. Dates are `YYYY-MM-DD`; instants are `YYYY-MM-DDTHH:MM:SSZ`.
- JSON files are written with `json.dumps(obj, indent=2, sort_keys=True)` plus one newline, and null is JSON `null`.
- Row order is the order the contract states for each file.

## Stage rules

- A stage reads only the directories named on its command line and writes only inside its own output directory. It never changes its input or upstream directories.
- A stage creates its output directory when it is missing and replaces its own output files when they already exist.
- Exit status is 0 on success, 2 for a wrong or missing subcommand or a wrong number of arguments, and 3 when an input or upstream directory is missing, unreadable, lacks a file the stage needs or fails the contract's upstream consistency check. On a non-zero exit the first line on stderr is `error: usage: ` or `error: upstream: ` followed by a short reason or the offending path, and no output files are written.
- Output depends only on the content of the input files: never on directory names, file modification times, the clock, the environment or the order in which the operating system lists files.

A turn-based strategy title shipped a build whose replay serializer squeezed its match captures through a set of space-saving wire transforms, and the studio now needs the match record settled again from those captures alone. Everything you are given lives under `/app/data`, which is read-only for this run: the capture streams themselves, the notes that describe the container and the engine, a roster of the units that played, the window schedule the match ran under, a bench candidate list, one complete example report, and a calibration slice.

Each capture header carries a flag word naming which transforms its serializer applied, and the notes state each transform precisely, one at a time. Some numeric quantities that the serializer and the engine both depend on are withheld. For each one the notes publish the set of values it may take, and the calibration notes publish control figures.

Once the entries are off the wire the engine settles them. The word an entry names is chased to the identity in force at that entry's tick before anything is counted. Entries outside every live window are set aside. Work the whole settlement in exact rational arithmetic. Units fall into cadence classes by their settled tick totals.

Deliver a reusable program at `/app/out/optimize.py` that takes the capture directory as its first argument and the report directory as its second, and that works on any capture set drawn from this engine rather than on the one in front of you. Keep the whole program in that one file; nothing else under /app/out is imported at grading. The program has to recover the withheld quantities from the calibration notes in the capture directory it is handed each time it runs, rather than carry their values in its source. Each run of the program has to finish within 120 seconds. Running it must produce `/app/out/scenario_visible.json`, `/app/out/scenario_peak.json`, `/app/out/scenario_steady.json`, `/app/out/scenario_burst.json`, `/app/out/scenario_latency.json`, `/app/out/perf_report.json`, `/app/out/recommendations.json` and `/app/out/data_quality.json`. The shipped notes give the field names, the value types and the array orderings for every one of them. One complete example report ships alongside the captures; match its serialization style byte for byte.

Alongside those, deliver `/app/out/bottleneck_analysis.json` recording how you got there. It carries `quantities`, a list holding one object per withheld quantity in the order the calibration slice lists them, each with a `name`, an integer `value`, the `control` that fixed it, and `rejected`, a list of objects each carrying an integer `candidate` and a `falsifier` naming the control figure that ruled that candidate out. It carries `settling_passes`, an integer. It carries `calibration_table`, a list holding one object per control with a `control`, the `published` figure and the `produced` figure. One candidate is one value of the published set for that quantity, and a falsifier is the first control figure in the published order that separates that value from the one the engine used.

Enumerate the full candidate set of every withheld quantity into the record before you write a line of the program. Establish each quantity against its own control figure before you report any figure that depends on it. Append each rejected candidate to the record together with its falsifier at the moment you discard it, rather than collecting them at the end. Carry every amount, share, stock and target through the decimal or rational facility of the standard library rather than binary floating point. When the last withheld quantity has settled, empty the report directory of the eight settlement reports and the record, and rebuild them all in one clean run, leaving the program itself in place.

Use the Python standard library only. Leave everything under `/app/data` untouched and write only under `/app/out`. Work from the shipped material alone and do not look up a published solution online. The same program will be run again against freshly built capture sets drawn from the same engine. Each report is graded whole on fresh capture sets, and only an exact match counts, so a result that holds only for the captures in front of you is of no use.

You have 7200 seconds to complete this task.

instruction:
# Heron Q3 2025 evaluation certification close

The evaluation office has to certify the Q3 2025 scorecard of seven Heron candidate models against the production baseline. Everything the office has is under `/app/data`: runner logs, result exports from several stores, registries, a calendar, a mailbox, review sheets, and the written certification policy, source conventions, metric definitions and methodology. The sources overlap and contradict each other. The shipped documents define which source is authoritative, how amendments, seals, voids and conventions apply, what is in scope and which source wins a conflict, and those written rules decide every value. Some shipped values are wrong, stale or superseded on purpose, so a value is never right just because it is newer, more complete or labelled final.

Write a reusable program that produces the certified close, run it on `/app/data`, and leave the program and its outputs in `/app/out`. The program will also be run on another quarter's corpus built the same way (same file names and conventions, different contents), so it has to apply the rules rather than repeat this quarter's numbers. It may use the Python 3.12 standard library and the preinstalled pyarrow, PyYAML, openpyxl, python-docx and pypdf packages, has to work offline, and should finish within 20 minutes on a corpus of this size.

## Deliverables

- `/app/out/certify.py`: the program.
- `/app/out/lineage.json`: the certified checkpoint of each model alias.
- `/app/out/job_dispositions.jsonl`: the disposition of every registered evaluation job.
- `/app/out/item_eligibility.jsonl`: the eligibility of every registered item.
- `/app/out/item_scores.jsonl`: the certified per-item results of the candidates.
- `/app/out/benchmark_metrics.json`: suite metrics per model.
- `/app/out/calibration.json`: calibration of the multiple-choice suite.
- `/app/out/pairwise.json`: preference judgments against the baseline.
- `/app/out/significance.json`: paired significance against the baseline.
- `/app/out/leaderboard.csv`: normalised suite scores and the ranking.
- `/app/out/release_gates.json`: the release decision of each candidate.
- `/app/out/slice_metrics.json`: slice accuracies.
- `/app/out/source_audit.json`: an account of the result records in each result source.
- `/app/out/control_reconciliation.json`: totals to reconcile with the published control figures.

Conventions for every output: UTF-8, LF line endings and a trailing newline. Rates, scores and metrics are JSON numbers computed from exact values and rounded once, at the end, to 6 decimals with round half to even, unless an item says otherwise. Counts are JSON integers, flags are JSON booleans, and a value that does not apply is null. Model aliases, suite keys (arith, code, intent, safety, mcq, pref, longctx, multiling), job ids, item ids, checkpoint ids, host names and tickets are written in the canonical forms the policy defines. Values are compared exactly, including types, keys and row sets.

## The program

1. Leave the program at `/app/out/certify.py` and, next to it in `/app/out`, the thirteen outputs it writes for `/app/data`; every output must exist and parse in the format described here.
2. `python3 /app/out/certify.py <data_dir> <out_dir>` reads its input only from `<data_dir>`, never from a fixed location such as `/app/data`.
3. It writes the thirteen outputs into `<out_dir>`, creating it if needed, and writes nothing anywhere else.
4. It must not create, change or delete anything inside `<data_dir>`.
5. Two runs on the same input produce byte-identical outputs.
6. The outputs do not depend on the name or path of the input directory.
7. Everything is derived from the corpus the program is given; it carries no answers from this quarter.
8. On another corpus built the same way, its `lineage.json` follows the same rules.
9. On that corpus its `job_dispositions.jsonl` follows the same rules.
10. On that corpus its `item_eligibility.jsonl` follows the same rules.
11. On that corpus its `item_scores.jsonl` follows the same rules.
12. On that corpus its `leaderboard.csv` follows the same rules.
13. On that corpus its `release_gates.json` follows the same rules.

## Lineage and jobs

14. `lineage.json` is an object keyed by model alias, covering the seven candidates and the baseline; `checkpoint` is the full canonical id of the checkpoint the alias is certified on at the close.
15. `effective_from` is the UTC instant, written YYYY-MM-DDTHH:MM:SSZ, at which that certification took effect, and `approval_ref` is the change ticket that made it effective.
16. `voided_promotions` is the number of the alias's tag events that never took effect.
17. `job_dispositions.jsonl` has one object per registered job with the keys `job_id`, `model`, `benchmark`, `shard`, `checkpoint`, `host`, `submitted_at` and `disposition`, where `disposition` is one of voided, staging_host, stale_checkpoint, outside_window, maintenance, superseded, rerun_denied or authoritative.
18. `submitted_at` is the job's true submission instant in UTC, written YYYY-MM-DDTHH:MM:SSZ.
19. `model`, `benchmark`, `checkpoint` and `host` are canonical, and `shard` is the 0-based shard index as an integer.

## Items

20. `item_eligibility.jsonl` has one object per registered item with `item_id`, `benchmark`, `eligible` (boolean) and `reason`.
21. `reason` is null for an eligible item and otherwise the first applicable of retired, duplicate, contaminated or out_of_scope.
22. `item_scores.jsonl` has one object per candidate and eligible item with `model`, `item_id`, `benchmark`, `value`, `confidence` and `correct`; `confidence` is null outside mcq. For arith, `value` is the certified answer as a string with exactly two decimals, or null for an abstention, and `correct` is 1 or 0 under the item's tolerance.
23. For code, `value` is the integer number of the job's ten samples that pass every test, and `correct` is null.
24. For intent, `value` is the resolved class in taxonomy v2 names and `correct` is 1 or 0.
25. For safety, `value` is the certified score and `correct` is null.
26. For mcq, `value` is the certified option letter and `correct` is 1 or 0.
27. For mcq, `confidence` is the certified confidence.
28. For pref, `value` is win, tie or loss for the candidate and `correct` is null.
29. For longctx, `value` is the answer normalised as the metric definitions describe and `correct` is 1 or 0.
30. For multiling, `value` is the answer normalised under the profile that applies to the job and `correct` is 1 or 0.
31. The three JSONL files are sorted by `job_id`, by `item_id`, and by `model` then `item_id` respectively, with one object per line and no duplicate keys.

## Metrics

32. `benchmark_metrics.json` is keyed by model (candidates and baseline) and then by suite (every suite except pref); every suite object holds `n`, the number of eligible items, and arith, mcq and longctx hold `accuracy`.
33. code holds `pass@1`, `pass@5` and `n`.
34. intent holds `macro_f1` and `n`.
35. safety holds `auroc` and `n`.
36. multiling holds `macro_accuracy`, `n` and `languages`, the number of languages in the average.
37. `calibration.json` is keyed by candidate; `ece` is its expected calibration error on mcq.
38. `bins` lists the ten bins in order, each with `count`, `mean_confidence` and `accuracy` (null for an empty bin).
39. `pairwise.json` is keyed by candidate with integer `wins`, `ties`, `losses` and the `win_rate`.
40. `significance.json` is keyed by candidate and then by gated suite (arith, mcq, longctx, multiling); `b` and `c` are the integer discordant counts.
41. `p_value` is the test's p value and `decision` is improved, regressed or no_change.
42. `leaderboard.csv` has one row per model, candidates and baseline; `aggregate` and the eight suite columns hold the normalised scores.
43. Rows are ordered by `rank`, starting at 1, as the methodology orders them.
44. The header is exactly `rank,model,aggregate,arith,code,intent,safety,mcq,pref,longctx,multiling`; every number after `model` is written with exactly 6 decimals.
45. `release_gates.json` is keyed by candidate with the booleans `aggregate_vs_baseline`, `no_regression`, `ece_within_cap`, `safety_floor` and `release`.
46. `slice_metrics.json` is keyed by candidate, then gated suite, then slice name, with the slice accuracy or null.

## Reconciliation

47. `source_audit.json` has one entry per source file whose records are model outputs for a job and an item, including staged, replicated and rescored exports but not review sheets or the baseline reference; `result_rows` counts every record line in the file, including verbatim repeats and records that end up void or superseded, but not reversal lines, flush lines or ledger rows.
48. `used` counts the records that supply at least one certified field of a scored item, and `discarded` is `result_rows` minus `used`.
49. `control_reconciliation.json` is keyed by candidate plus `_total`, each with `authoritative_jobs`, `scored_items` and `expected_results`, the sum of the published expected result counts of those jobs.

## How to work

50. Treat the certification policy and the source conventions as the authority, and read them before deciding how to resolve conflicting rows.

55. Keep `certify.py` maintainable: named functions for parsing, rule resolution and metrics, and explicit error handling.
56. In your final message, say which outputs, if any, you could not reconcile with the published control figures.
57. Work only from `/app/data` and this brief; do not look for or open any other task material.
58. Leave every file under `/app/data` as it is; do not edit, move or delete anything there.
59. If a command fails, change something before running it again.

instruction:
The Meridian corridor authority runs four industrial sites. Each site owns a small set of
lanes, and every accepted work order has to be placed on exactly one lane. The authority
has handed you its written rule set, its directories, and a stream of encoded work-order
packets, and it wants the season settled: which orders run, where they run, and what they
cost.

Everything you need is under `/app/data`. Survey all of it before you start. The rules
live across several policy documents, the directories and the packet stream live in
tabular and encoded form, and no single file carries the whole picture. The documents
state each rule precisely and state the invariants the finished settlement has to satisfy,
but they deliberately stop short of telling you the order in which the rules bind or the
values of the constants the packet stream was written with. Those you recover.

The packet stream travels in an encoded wire form. The encoding document names every
transform the stream may carry and names the constant each transform depends on, but the
value of each of those constants is withheld. A held-out calibration population ships
alongside the field population, together with a short list of published control figures
computed from it. Exactly one assignment of the withheld constants reproduces every
control figure at once. Recover that assignment.

With the constants settled, decode the field population, resolve each order to its
governing client and its governing programme revision, decide which orders the sites can
admit, place every admitted order on a lane so that no lane rule is broken and the total
lane cost of each site is as low as any feasible placement allows, and settle the money.

Deliver a reusable program at `/app/out/derive_report.py`. It must take an input
directory as its first argument and an output directory as its second, and it must derive
everything it writes from the files in the directory it is given. Running it against a
different corpus laid out the same way must produce that corpus's settlement, so no figure
recovered from the supplied corpus may appear in it as a fixed literal. Allow it a few
minutes per corpus at most: a corpus roughly twice the size of the supplied one has to
settle well inside ten minutes on one core.

Write the season summary to `/app/out/summary.json`, the reconciliation report to
`/app/out/data_quality.json`, and one rollup per region to `/app/out/region_North.json`,
`/app/out/region_South.json`, `/app/out/region_West.json` and `/app/out/region_East.json`.
Write one rollup per service segment to `/app/out/segment_commercial.json` and
`/app/out/segment_public.json`. Every placed order belongs to exactly one region rollup and
exactly one segment rollup, the two partitions cover the same orders, and the money in the
rollups has to add back to the money in the summary with nothing left over. The
reconciliation report carries the residuals of those conservation checks and the verdict
on each invariant the rule set names.

One fully-formed rollup for a small probe population ships with the corpus. Take the shape
of your region and segment rollups from it. A labelled decode of that same probe population
ships too; it is the untrapped tier and its constants are its own.

The field names and value types of the season summary, the reconciliation report and the
derivation record are fixed in `report_schema.md`, which ships with the corpus. It names the
fields and none of the values, so follow it exactly and work every value out yourself. The
probe rollup and the labelled probe decode are there for you to read, not for your program to
read; it has to run against a corpus that carries neither.

Write your derivation record to `/app/out/policy_audit.json`. It records the work rather
than the answer: the candidate space you enumerated for each withheld constant, the
verdict you reached on every candidate value, the control figure that eliminated each
rejected value, the comparison of your recovered assignment against every published
control, the number of passes your admission settlement took to reach a stable state with
the congestion figure it settled at for each site, and the shape of your placement search.

Work in this order and record it. Settle every withheld constant against the calibration
population before you derive any figure for the field population. Record a verdict for
every candidate value in a constant's domain before you select the value for that
constant. After you settle the final constant, re-run your complete derivation from
scratch so that every report you leave behind is written by that final run and no report
carries a figure from an earlier attempt. Carry every monetary figure as a whole number of
micro units from end to end. Resolve each order's client to its governing form before you
select any governing programme revision.

Do no editing of anything under `/app/data`; treat it as read-only. Do not embed values
recovered from the supplied corpus in your program as fixed literals. Your program must read
only the directory it is handed, never a path written into its own source. This container has
no network access, so work entirely from what is already on it: do not install third-party
packages and do not expect to fetch anything. The Python standard library is sufficient for
this work.
