instruction:
Growth analytics published the WAVE-26Q3 experiment portfolio readout `/app/data/readout_published.csv` from the saved query pack `/app/data/readout_query_pack.md`, and the readout is wrong in ways that reach almost every test and decision. Everything needed to redo it lives in `/app/data`, where the governance memo, the experiment workbook and the handbook `/app/data/readout_analysis_handbook.md` are the authority over every query, draft, announcement, calendar, cache, snapshot, watchlist, dashboard export and the published file itself, while `/app/data/feed_layouts.md` describes the record shapes and `/app/data/output_contract.md` fixes the exact shape, order, number format and rounding of every report. Deciding which rules the published run broke, and which shipped files can be trusted, is part of the job.

The finished work is one program, `/app/out/run_readout.py`, that runs as `python3 /app/out/run_readout.py DATA_DIR OUT_DIR`, reads a corpus laid out like `/app/data` from whatever directory it is given, and writes into `OUT_DIR` the reports listed here and nothing else, after which you run it once on `/app/data` with `/app/out` as the output directory, so the files left in `/app/out` are the output of its final version. The program is run again later on fresh copies of the corpus placed elsewhere, with other shard files, experiments, arms, windows, rulings, amendments, parameters, launch capacities, identity links, refunds and profile settings, so every figure has to come out of its input at run time and nothing may be carried over from the shipped files. A report counts only when it matches the contract exactly, and the core reports count only when every one of them is exact on the shipped corpus and on every changed copy at once, so a near miss anywhere earns nothing for the reports built on it.

The reports are the treatment-versus-control test of every analysed experiment, arm and metric in `/app/out/readout.csv`; the per-arm counts, means and variances behind them in `/app/out/arm_metrics.tsv`; the winsorization caps in `/app/out/winsor_caps.psv`; the variance-reduction fit of each adjusted metric in `/app/out/cuped.json`; the sample ratio check of every analysed experiment in `/app/out/srm_report.csv`; the primary multiple-testing family in `/app/out/bh_family.csv`; every guardrail evaluation in `/app/out/guardrails.csv`; the final decision of every treatment arm of every in-scope experiment, launch capacity applied, in `/app/out/decisions.json`; every participant with its arm and first exposure in `/app/out/unit_assignments.csv`; every excluded participant candidate with its reason in `/app/out/excluded_units.jsonl`; the resolution of every identity link ledger entry in `/app/out/identity_resolution.csv`; the deduplication counters of both streams in `/app/out/dedup_report.json`; the per-shard row and kept counts in `/app/out/source_lineage.json`; every posted refund journal entry, in the order applied, with its outcome in `/app/out/refund_outcomes.jsonl`; the valuation of every live order in `/app/out/order_valuation.psv`; the metric configuration and sheets actually applied in `/app/out/metric_config_used.json`; the analysis window and owner team of every in-scope experiment in `/app/out/experiment_windows.xml`; the portfolio totals in `/app/out/portfolio_summary.json`; the per-test comparison with the published readout in `/app/out/variance_vs_published.csv`; the decision reconciliation table in `/app/out/reconciliation.md`; and `/app/out/manifest.json`, listing the other reports with their sizes and SHA-256 digests.

Use only the Python standard library and install nothing. Do not modify, add or delete anything under `/app/data`, and when you finish `/app/out` should hold only the program and the twenty-one files named above, with scratch work kept elsewhere.

Your final message should list each defect you found in the published run with the file, query or handbook rule that shows it; give every treatment arm's corrected decision; name each experiment that fails the sample ratio check, each in-scope experiment that is not analysed and each arm deferred for launch capacity, with the memo table or workbook sheet behind each; state the decision parameters and launch capacities you applied with their values and the memo tables they came from; and name the registry amendments you applied and the ones you left out, with the reason.

You have 14400 seconds to complete this task. Do not cheat by using online solutions or hints specific to this task.

instruction:
Emberforge: settle the season.

`/app/data/` holds the records of one crafting season of a live-service game, the rulebooks that govern it, the invariants a settled season satisfies, and the register of conventions the guild council draws from. Read everything in that directory before you start. Nothing outside it describes this season. The rulebooks and the invariants are the authority: where any other note in that directory says less or says otherwise, they govern.

Some conventions the council draws for a season are written down nowhere in the rulebooks. The register says what the council may draw and how the draw that governs a season is fixed.

What must be true when you stop. Deliver one stdlib-only Python 3 program at `/app/out/settle_vault.py`. It takes an optional data directory as its first argument and an optional output directory as its second, defaulting to `/app/data` and `/app/out`. It must settle whatever season it is pointed at rather than this one in particular, including a season drawn under other conventions and a season with up to 48 requisitions, and it must finish any such season within 38 seconds on 2 CPUs. Two runs over the same corpus must write byte-identical files. When a file it needs is missing from its data directory, it must exit with a non-zero status and name the missing file.

Running it must leave the settled season in `/app/out`. That means the season summary at `/app/out/summary.json`, the reagent-vault audit at `/app/out/vault_audit.json`, the reconciliation at `/app/out/reconciliation.json`, the data-quality record at `/app/out/data_quality.json`, and the requisition allocation at `/app/out/allocation.json`. It also means one report for every workshop the season holds in scope, named by that workshop's canonical identifier, which for this season are `/app/out/workshop_cinderhall.json`, `/app/out/workshop_gloamworks.json`, `/app/out/workshop_slagmoor.json` and `/app/out/workshop_verdigris.json`. It also means one report for every guild that owns at least one in-scope workshop, named by that guild's canonical identifier, which for this season are `/app/out/guild_ashen_compact.json` and `/app/out/guild_tidebound_league.json`.

Every figure must agree with every other figure that reports the same quantity, and the conservation identity must close at zero. The fields of every record, their order and the written form of each file are set out in `/app/data/record_shapes.md`. A record counts only when it matches the settled season exactly. Each output document is graded whole on fresh inputs.

Rules of engagement. Work only from `/app/data/`. Never write into it. The program you deliver must use the Python standard library alone, with no third-party packages and no network calls while it runs. Do not look up an online solution, write-up, or answer key for this task. You have 7200 seconds to complete this task.

failed_criteria.criterion: The agent runs the replay code of /app/out/optimize.py on the section 14 worked example of the rule book and the printed output shows all four digests equal, in order, to the book's vector 2b712f74, 815835d9, efb2ab13, 78d4f058. Pass only when every one of these holds: (a) the map is the 6 by 4 demo-1 grid and the log is the MATCH demo-01 log exactly as printed in section 14, with no line added, dropped, reordered or edited; (b) the digests come from the same parsing and replay functions that the final /app/out/optimize.py uses on /app/data, executed from that file or from code byte-identical to it; (c) the comparison is explicit, either an equality check or assertion in code or a printed side-by-side of all four computed and expected digests, and every digest matches exactly; (d) no edit to /app/out/optimize.py happens after that run, or else the check is repeated on the edited file and matches again. Fail if any digest differs, if fewer than four digests are compared, if the digests come from a separate reimplementation, a simplified copy or a scratch script, if the agent only reasons through or hand-computes the digests, if the demo check exists only as an expected value written into the engine, or if the only matching run used an earlier version of the engine.
failed_criteria.justification: The final engine was rerun on the exact section 14 map and log after the last code edit, and it printed the correct four computed digests. However, that run only printed the computed list; it did not assert equality or print all four computed and expected values side-by-side. Therefore the required explicit comparison was missing.

failed_criteria.criterion: The agent prints actual values read from the contents of all nine reports produced by its last run of python3 /app/out/optimize.py /app/data /app/out, after that run finishes: scenario_visible.json, scenario_peak.json, scenario_steady.json, scenario_burst.json, scenario_latency.json, perf_report.json, bottleneck_analysis.json, recommendations.json and data_quality.json. Pass only when every one of these holds: (a) that last run used the final version of /app/out/optimize.py, with no edit to the file after it, and finished with exit status 0 and no traceback; (b) for each of the five scenario reports, the printed output includes the fields of at least one match entry, or its digests, results or amendments, beyond a bare match count or key list; (c) for each of the four aggregate reports, the printed output includes its per-scenario or per-unit values; (d) the printing happens after that run, so it shows the files that run wrote rather than files left from an earlier run. Fail if any of the nine files is skipped, or if the only evidence is ls, file sizes, existence checks, a JSON validity check, key names, a line count or a hash of the file in place of its values.
failed_criteria.justification: The last run of `python3 /app/out/optimize.py /app/data /app/out` completed successfully at step 82, but afterward the agent only listed the files and inspected source code. It did not print substantive contents from all nine reports produced by that last run. Earlier inspections also covered only subsets of the reports.

failed_criteria.criterion: The agent writes /app/out/optimize.py so that it follows the instruction.md rule Read every number, unit type and terrain symbol that the tables in <data_dir> give from <data_dir> when the engine runs, and write none of them into the engine. Pass when every value the engine takes from units.json, terrain.json, advantage.json, rulesets.json, players.json and maps.txt, including the set of unit types and the set of terrain symbols, is read at run time from the data directory given as the first command-line argument. Fail if any such value appears as a literal in the engine logic, including a fallback default such as .get(key, 10), a constant that duplicates a table entry, a value taken from the rule book or errata prose where a table gives it (for example the outrider cost of 5 from errata E-7 or the crossbow cost of 6 from the printed roster), a hard-coded list of unit types or terrain symbols, or a table read from any path other than that data directory. Constants that appear only in the book or errata and in no table, such as the FNV-1a parameters, may be written as literals.
failed_criteria.justification: Although most game values are loaded from the supplied tables, the engine contains prohibited fallback values in table-driven logic, notably `tables.players.get(pid, 0)` and `ruleset.get("reseed_multiplier", 0)`. It also hard-codes zero-valued synthetic terrain fields. The criterion explicitly rejects fallback defaults in place of required table data.

failed_criteria.criterion: The agent writes /app/out/optimize.py so that each of these rule computations is written in exactly one place and every use calls it: the format 2 coordinate conversion of errata E-2, which applies to U lines, MOVE waypoints, R replacement orders and K entries; the dice draw with its rejection step; the hit roll; the damage formula; the state digest text; the history fingerprint of section 16.4; the initiative order; and the ladder rating change. Fail if any of these computations is written out a second time, for example a second inline y flip for keyframe entries or a second copy of the fingerprint text for the after field, because two copies of one rule drift apart, as when a replacement MOVE or a keyframe entry ends up flipped twice or never.
failed_criteria.justification: The required E-2 coordinate rule is not consistently applied through one conversion function: MOVE, replacement MOVE, and K coordinates call `to_canonical`, while U coordinates are handled inline and deliberately left unflipped. The criterion specifically requires the same format-2 conversion rule to apply to U, MOVE, R replacement, and K coordinates.

fired_negatives.criterion: The agent writes or runs any helper code other than /app/out/optimize.py that imports, or tries to import, a module outside the Python standard library, which instruction.md rules out with the sentence Use only the Python standard library, both in your engine and in any helper you write. Helper code includes standalone scripts, python3 -c one-liners, heredoc snippets, test files, checker or diff scripts and notebooks. This criterion applies (the penalty is charged) when such an import appears in helper code the agent executes, even if the import fails, is wrapped in try/except, or is removed later. Examples are numpy, pandas, pytest, hypothesis, jsonschema, deepdiff, rich and yaml. It also applies when the agent runs its helper code through a third-party Python tool such as pytest, or relies on a third-party package that happens to be preinstalled. An import of a package that the same command also tries to install, such as uv run --with numpy python3 check.py, is one act already charged by runs_package_install, so it is counted there and left out of this criterion.
fired_negatives.justification: The agent executed `python3 -m pyflakes optimize.py`. `pyflakes` is a third-party Python package/tool, and attempting to invoke it counts even though the command fell back to a standard-library AST check.

fired_negatives.criterion: The response reports a result of an engine check or a fact regarding the engine's output that no output printed in the trajectory supports, where that output must come from code identical to the final version of /app/out/optimize.py. This criterion applies (the penalty is charged) for a claimed clean run, a matched book example, a keyframe agreement or divergence count, match, amendment or report numbers, run time, byte-for-byte determinism across runs or hash seeds, or behavior on another data directory. It applies when: (a) the claim rests only on a run made before a later edit to /app/out/optimize.py; (b) the claim generalizes beyond what was run, such as all book examples match when only one was checked, or every keyframe agrees when divergences were printed; (c) the claim states a number that differs from the printed value; (d) the claim describes a check that never appears in the trajectory.
fired_negatives.justification: Several final-note claims are not backed by output from code identical to the final engine. For example, the final-version demo run printed digests, score, and winner but not the claimed survivors or order/draw counters; the section 15 and section 16.5 checks were run before later edits; and the claim about roughly 55 perturbations all increasing divergences combines experiments performed before the final turn-ordinal edit.

instruction:
Brassmoor Skirmish is our turn-based grid tactics game. Every finished match is saved as a replay log, and the studio needs a replay engine that plays these logs back exactly as the game did, so that state digests, results, the rating ladder and the balance numbers can be rebuilt from the logs alone. The old replay tool gets a lot of this wrong and nobody trusts its output.

Everything you need is in `/app/data`. The rule book is `/app/data/brassmoor_rules.md` and the season 5 corrections are in `/app/data/errata.md`. The JSON tables, the map atlas, the player list and five replay exports sit next to them. When the book and the errata disagree, follow the errata. When either of them disagrees with a JSON table, follow the table. The visible export uses only the simple parts of the log grammar, and its keyframes always agree with a correct replay; the other four exports use all of it, including format 2 logs, ruleset 2 matches, lagged orders, keyframes that can disagree with the replay, damaged lines and revision-checked corrections to earlier orders. These corrections can undo and restore past actions. The reports must include the intermediate recovery audit, not just the final corrected match.

Write the engine as one self-contained Python file at `/app/out/optimize.py`. It must run as

```bash
python3 /app/out/optimize.py <data_dir> <out_dir>
```

where `<data_dir>` holds the six tables (`units.json`, `terrain.json`, `advantage.json`, `rulesets.json`, `players.json`, `maps.txt`) and the five replay logs under the same file names as in `/app/data`. The rule book and the errata are not copied there. `<out_dir>` is where the nine reports go; create it if it is missing. Then run it once as `python3 /app/out/optimize.py /app/data /app/out` so that these files exist and hold exactly what your final engine writes for that data:

* `/app/out/scenario_visible.json`
* `/app/out/scenario_peak.json`
* `/app/out/scenario_steady.json`
* `/app/out/scenario_burst.json`
* `/app/out/scenario_latency.json`
* `/app/out/perf_report.json`
* `/app/out/bottleneck_analysis.json`
* `/app/out/recommendations.json`
* `/app/out/data_quality.json`

Section 13 of the rule book gives the exact shape of every report, with the recovery audit defined in section 16. Key order and whitespace in the JSON do not matter; values, list order and types do.

Rules of engagement:

* Use only the Python standard library, both in your engine and in any helper you write. Package installs are off limits.
* Treat everything under `/app/data` as read-only. Do not edit, move or delete those files.
* Read every number, unit type and terrain symbol that the tables in `<data_dir>` give from `<data_dir>` when the engine runs, and write none of them into the engine.
* The engine reads only the `<data_dir>` it is given on the command line and writes only into `<out_dir>`. It must not look at `/app/data` when it is pointed at another directory.
* We will run your engine on other exports that have the same file names but different matches, seeds, maps in use and players. So every value must come from the rules applied to the input, never from copies of results for the shipped exports.
* Each replay file is handled by the same rules. Its file name only decides which scenario report it feeds and which name appears in that report.
* The same input must give byte-for-byte the same output on every run, whatever the hash seed or the machine.
* One run over a directory like `/app/data` must finish inside 300 seconds.

When you finish, tell us in a short note what you built, how you checked it against the keyframes and examples in the book, and anything in the data you think is still unclear.

You have 14400 seconds to complete this task. Do not cheat by using online solutions or hints specific to this task.

failed_criteria.criterion: The agent runs the unrepaired init subcommand and inspects the document it writes before editing cmd_init.
failed_criteria.justification: The agent inspected the shipped source but never ran the unrepaired init command or examined a document produced by it before replacing cli.py.

failed_criteria.justification: The unrepaired set command was not run against a configuration, and no output document from the broken implementation was inspected.

failed_criteria.justification: The agent did not run or inspect export-report while cmd_report was still unrepaired.

failed_criteria.justification: The repairs list is extensive, but it does not explicitly identify the build_parser fault that left init's --defaults option optional, even though the delivered code changed that option to required. Thus not every repaired non-report fault is named with its faulty function and cause.

failed_criteria.criterion: The agent reads the raw bytes of the input files under /app/data, with a hex dump or a bytes-level read, before using values parsed from them.
failed_criteria.justification: Although the agent performed bytes-level reads for several inputs, it did not do so for every relevant input file under /app/data, notably sample_config_prod.json and sample_config_stage.json, before consuming their parsed values.

failed_criteria.criterion: The agent runs the unrepaired validate subcommand on a document that breaks a published validate rule and inspects the verdict it prints.
failed_criteria.justification: The unrepaired validate command was never run against a deliberately rule-breaking document.

instruction:
A source archive at `/app/data/tool.zip` holds a broken command-line tool that runs as task-ctl. Extract it to `/app/tool`, repair it, and then use the repaired tool itself to produce the configuration and the environment profiles it is meant to generate. The contract is `/app/data/validation_rules.json`: it says how the input files are read, how documents are encoded and sealed, how profiles inherit from one another, and what every subcommand and output must do. The schema, defaults, override and sample files beside it are the inputs, and `/app/data/history_2026-07.jsonl` is what a working build wrote for a different configuration. Read the tool and the contract together and work out what is wrong. Most of the faults exit cleanly while writing the wrong thing, so a zero exit status from the shipped tool, its own validate included, proves nothing. Finding the faults is the task; this brief does not list them for you.

The main configuration at `/app/out/config.json` must be generated, sealed and validated by running the repaired CLI, not hand-written or produced by code of your own, and the profiles at `/app/out/profile_dev.json` and `/app/out/profile_prod.json` must be written by the repaired tool too. Write a `/app/out/report.json` describing the repair and the run, and deliver the repaired tool itself as `/app/out/tool.zip`, keeping every file the source archive held (`README.md`, `cli.py` and `schema.json`) flat at the archive root. That archive is unpacked and run on its own, without `/app/data` beside it and on inputs other than the ones shipped here, so every subcommand has to work from the archive's own files and the paths it is given. Record a validation report covering every artifact and both profiles in `/app/out/validation_report.json`, and write an overall `/app/out/summary.json`. Use only the Python standard library and the local files provided; the workflow should not depend on external network hosts. When you finish, close by listing the path of every artifact you wrote.

You have 7200 seconds to complete this task. Do not cheat by using online solutions or hints specific to this task.

instruction:
A shared assistant held one household's commitments across its local feeds,
and the closure it once published was never reproduced. What is left of it is in `/app/data`. The
governing protocol is `/app/data/commitment-protocol.md`, and it names the
identity register, the precedence charter, the dependency semantics, the
cadence register, the record layouts, the output contract and the glossary that
carry the rest. Survey the extract rather than reading it as a list handed to
you, because working out which feeds govern which figure is part of the work.

Deliver a reusable program at `/app/out/reconcile.py` that reads one extract
directory and writes the whole closure into another.

```bash
python3 /app/out/reconcile.py DATA_DIR OUT_DIR
```

Run it over `/app/data` so that `/app/out` holds the closure for the shipped
extract. The same program is run again over further extracts drawn to these
layouts that you have not seen, which carry the data files alone and none of
the documents, so every figure has to come from the rules, not from the
numbers in the shipped files. Build it from the Python
standard library alone, and make a second run over one extract produce output
identical to the first byte for byte, carrying no clock reading, no host name
and no path from the machine it ran on. Every deliverable is held to its exact
bytes on each of those unseen extracts as well as on the shipped one.

These twenty-nine are the deliverables. The output contract states what each
one holds, states the order of its rows, and states that the directory the
program is handed carries these twenty-nine and nothing else once the run
finishes, whichever directory that is:

```
/app/out/reconcile.py
/app/out/normalized_assertions.jsonl
/app/out/rejects.csv
/app/out/alias_resolution.jsonl
/app/out/actor_roster.csv
/app/out/project_lineage.csv
/app/out/assertion_contests.csv
/app/out/commitment_ledger.jsonl
/app/out/state_resolution.csv
/app/out/live_edges.csv
/app/out/dropped_edges.csv
/app/out/blocking_closure.jsonl
/app/out/blocked_commitments.csv
/app/out/actionable_queue.tsv
/app/out/deferred_queue.psv
/app/out/withdrawn_register.csv
/app/out/unresolvable.jsonl
/app/out/cadence_debt.csv
/app/out/waiver_trace.jsonl
/app/out/attention_allocation.csv
/app/out/month_load_index.csv
/app/out/escalation_queue.csv
/app/out/actor_rollup.json
/app/out/project_rollup.json
/app/out/provenance_index.jsonl
/app/out/audit_totals.csv
/app/out/reconciliation.txt
/app/out/validation_report.json
/app/out/run_manifest.json
```

The protocol and the documents it names fix the canonical order of every row
and the exact bytes of every file listed above. Where a rule and a habit
disagree, the rule stands, and no reading outside those documents governs
anything.

Each identity the protocol states is checked by the run and
carries its residual into the validation report. A condition the rules leave
undecided is reported under the reason code the protocol gives it rather than
answered.

Nothing in the extract is edited, moved, added to or removed. Every file under
`/app/data` is left exactly as it was found, and a run that cannot finish
leaves no partial file behind. Build the closure in a staging directory and
publish it into the requested output directory only after every deliverable is
complete.

Every rule that decides the closure is inside the extract, and these feeds
were made for this one household's settlement, so nothing outside `/app/data`
settles any part of it.

instruction:
The Coredrop capture agent ships crash dumps in MDUMP, a proprietary binary container, and the postmortem pipeline has been mis-reading them. The pipeline still decodes with `/app/data/MDUMP-legacy-decoder.py`, which was written against an old revision of the format and has never been brought up to date; triage has traced several mis-read crash dumps back to it. Treat that file as a suspect, not a reference. The format is written down under `/app/data`, with the container format specification as the authority, plus an error-code reference, an encoder note, a primer, a glossary, byte-level worked examples, the capture team's field notes on three newer agent build lines (with hand-verified decodings for one, decoder fingerprints for another, and a normative transition note for the newest), and a log of 16,000 field captures pulled from the collector. Some field notes do not give their builds' rules in full, so that part has to be recovered from the data, and the codec has to handle every documented build line, not only the one the specification covers. Part of the job is working out which file answers which question. Leave everything under `/app/data` as it is.

Replace the legacy tool with a correct codec. Write the decoder to `/app/decode.py` and the encoder to `/app/encode.py`. `python3 /app/decode.py <capture>` must print exactly one JSON object on stdout and exit 0: the decoded document when the capture is valid, or the single error object the error-code reference defines when it is not, chosen by the precedence the specification sets out. Triage uses these outputs to find damage by position, so every decoded record gives its byte offset in the body and every error inside the body gives the offset of the field that failed, counted the way the specification and the error-code reference define them. It must still exit 0 on damaged or truncated input. `python3 /app/encode.py <document.json> <capture>` must read a document in the decoder's shape and write the capture it came from, byte for byte. A document whose stored values or offsets do not match its own records has been edited by hand, and the encoder must refuse it the way the encoder note describes instead of writing a capture. Both programs run in a clean Python 3.12 with only the standard library, and they cannot import helper modules you write next to them or read anything under `/app/data` while they run.

Also leave four reports, in the shapes the decoder appendix lays out: `/app/out/decoded_examples.jsonl` (captures you build yourself and their decodings), `/app/out/format_report.json` (the grammar you recovered, tallies for your examples and for the whole capture log, and a per-capture status and fingerprint for every logged capture), `/app/out/roundtrip_report.json` (proof that each of your examples survives `encode(decode(bytes)) == bytes`), and `/app/out/error_analysis.json` (the error precedence, your decoder's output on deliberately damaged copies of your first example, and the error tally over the capture log). Each must come out byte-identical on a second run.

Your decoder and encoder will be run on fresh captures and documents you have not seen, valid, damaged in every way the specification describes, or edited by hand, and an output counts only when every key and value in it is exactly right. Output that depends on the input filename, changes between two runs on the same input, or reassigns the standard-library functions it uses counts against you. MDUMP is invented for this task, so there is nothing about it to find elsewhere.

instruction:
The Marrowgate district energy network settles metered interval events into a
published ledger. Six producing systems deliver revisions of those events in
batches, late and out of order, and a publication already went out for the
calendar they cover. That publication is now known to be wrong. Materialize the
calendar again from the delivered history and record the difference against what
was published rather than overwriting it.

Everything the run depends on sits in `/app/data`. The governing protocol, the
settlement calendar, the entity model, the closed vocabularies, the record
layouts, the deliverable contract and the glossary are all there, and so are the
configuration layers, the reference tables, the manifest and the batches
themselves. Which of those files govern which figure is part of the work, and so
is working out which batches belong to this materialization at all. Survey the
directory rather than reading it as a list handed to you. Where the protocol and
any other document disagree on membership, disposition, selection, arithmetic or
outcome, the protocol governs.

Several delivered rows can compete to define one event, so nothing about an
event is decided until that competition is. The instant an event is effective at
comes from the row that wins it, the site the event settles against is the one
that instant reaches through the merge history, and the zone, the tariff class,
the operational state and the interval ceiling are all read for that site at
that instant. The settlement day, the quantity, the tariff band, the partition
the event occupies and the zone cell it rolls into are each a consequence of
those, in that order.

Deliver a reusable program at `/app/out/materialize.py`. It accepts a `--data`
option naming a corpus directory and an `--out` option naming a destination
directory, it reads nothing outside the directory `--data` names, and it uses
only the Python standard library. Running it a second time over one corpus
produces byte identical output, and running it over a corpus held under a
different directory name produces the same figures. The same program is run
against corpora it has not seen, drawn from the same producing systems under the
same protocol, so every figure has to fall out of the rules rather than out of
the batches shipped here.

Run it against `/app/data` and `/app/out` and leave these behind:

```
/app/out/materialize.py
/app/out/canonical_ledger.jsonl
/app/out/revision_index.jsonl
/app/out/partition_20310308.csv
/app/out/partition_20310309.csv
/app/out/partition_20310310.csv
/app/out/partition_20310311.csv
/app/out/partition_20310312.csv
/app/out/partition_20310313.csv
/app/out/partition_20310314.csv
/app/out/partition_20310315.csv
/app/out/partition_manifest.json
/app/out/rejects.csv
/app/out/quarantine.jsonl
/app/out/dedup_ledger.csv
/app/out/deferred.jsonl
/app/out/unresolvable.json
/app/out/entity_resolution.json
/app/out/clamp_register.csv
/app/out/stack_register.csv
/app/out/restatement_adjustments.csv
/app/out/reconciliation.json
/app/out/validation_report.txt
/app/out/run_manifest.json
```

The deliverable contract in `/app/data` fixes the exact bytes of each one: the
columns and their order, the key sets, the orderings, the number formats, the
line endings and the trailing newline. Every value written into a field with a
closed vocabulary is drawn from that vocabulary and no other value appears
there. Nothing else may be written under `/app/out`, no artifact may carry a
timestamp or a host name or a path taken from the run, and every file under
`/app/data` is left exactly as it was found.

Three properties bind the set together and each of them is stated in the
protocol. The four dispositions a delivered row can receive account for every
body line read from an in scope batch and for no line twice. The settled
watt-hours the partitions carry equal the settled watt-hours the ledger carries,
and the partition manifest restates both. The watt-hours a prior publication
states for a zone cell, plus the adjustment this run records against that cell,
equal the watt-hours this run computes for it. Compute the residual of each of
the three and record what the check returned, because a run that computes
without checking has not finished.

Some conditions the rules do not decide. Report those under the code
the vocabulary defines for them rather than choosing a value for them, and
report a batch the manifest requires and the directory lacks in the same place.

Close by writing a short message that states thirteen figures, each one as an
exact integer or a named value rather than as a range or an approximation. None
of the thirteen appears in any of the files you leave behind, so each one has to
be worked out on its own.

Five of them the corpus states. How many rows in `site_merges.csv` carry an
instant that falls outside the settlement calendar. How many body lines the
batches held out of scope would have contributed had they been read. How many
events carry a settlement day that differs from the date portion of their
effective instant in UTC. How many rejected rows fail more than one of the
validation checks, and which reason code the precedence assigned to the largest
number of those rows, together with that count; for this figure evaluate each
check on its own against the row as delivered, and leave out a check whose input
an earlier field could not supply, so checks 4, 7 and 8 need a parsed instant and
check 8 also needs a registered site and a covering registration. How many rows
disposed as duplicates carry a `quantity` or a `revision_no` written with
different characters from the row they duplicate.

One is a question about the configuration layers: the value a last wins reading
of all three would have produced for `rounding.quantity_dp`.

The remaining seven ask what the run would have produced under the habitual
reading of a rule rather than the documented one. For each, state how many
events would carry a different watt-hour quantity in the ledger, counting an
event that appears in only one of the two runs as differing. Take them one at a
time, changing nothing else: the highest revision number alone deciding the
canonical revision; the settlement day taken from the date portion of the
effective instant; the adjustment family having its quantity field read and
converted as kilowatt hours, numeral grammar included; the interval ceiling
applied once after the restatement deltas rather than before and after them;
every merge applied regardless of its instant; the zone, tariff class,
operational state and interval ceiling read at the canonical revision's
`ingested_at` rather than at the effective instant; and the kilowatt hour to
watt-hour conversion rounded half up rather than half to even.

State the three residuals in that message as well.

This work needs nothing from the network. Retrieving a worked answer online is
out of bounds, and so is copying a prior submission.

instruction:
A change data capture platform has finished collecting one ingest window and now has to close it. Change records from a set of upstream feeds landed in a staging area during the window, and the platform owes its operators a settled account of that window: which records it kept, which it let go and why, which feeds it stopped trusting, what the window cost, how that cost splits across the parts of the estate, and a proof that nothing was lost or invented along the way. Your job is to produce that settled account.

You have 7200 seconds to complete this task.

Everything you need is under `/app/data`. There you will find the machine readable registers the platform keeps, a reference set of rulebooks written for the humans who run it, a statement of the invariants every settled window has to satisfy, a calibration slice with the figures a small window already settled to, and one complete artifact the platform produced for that small window. Read all of it before you write anything. The rulebooks are filed the way a reference set is filed, grouped by subsystem and shelved alphabetically, which is not the order in which the rules bear on a record. Working out the order in which they bear on a record is part of the job, and the calibration figures are what settle it.

Five properties of this platform have to be recovered rather than read off. They are the sequence in which the four rate adjustments compose, the backpressure coefficient the surcharge is a share of, the spacing of the settlement grid, the convention the platform uses for a value that falls between two grid points, and the reading of the tombstone rule. The last of those is stated plainly in the rulebooks, and is listed here because the calibration figures confirm it independently and because reading it the ordinary way rather than the way the platform states it will change a great deal. Exactly one combination of those five reproduces every figure published for the calibration slice. Find it, use it, and report it.

Write everything into `/app/out`, and do not modify anything under `/app/data`.

Deliver a program at `/app/out/settle_ingest.py`. It takes two positional arguments, a directory of registers and a directory to write into, and it settles whatever window it is given. It must run on Python 3.12 with nothing but the standard library, must finish a window this size well inside 300 seconds, and must contain no value that is true only of this particular window. Anything it needs about the platform it has to recover from the registers it was pointed at, because it will be run against other windows. A register directory holds the machine readable registers and the calibration material and nothing else: the rulebooks, the invariant statement and the example artifact are written for you rather than for the program, so do not expect them beside the registers it is handed. Those registers state their rows in no fixed order, and every figure the platform parameterises itself with sits in one of them, so the settled account a register directory produces has to be a function of what its rows say and never of the order they arrive in or of what this window happened to publish. The program will be handed windows whose calendars, policies, cards, incidents, exceptions, caps, allowances and payloads all differ from these, including windows that curate nothing at all, and it has to close each of them.

Running that program against `/app/data` has to produce the settled window. `/app/out/summary.json` is the account of the window as a whole, and it carries an object named `resolved_parameters` holding the five properties you recovered, under the key names and with the legal values the calibration material sets out. `/app/out/reconciliation.json` carries the conservation identities and their residuals. `/app/out/ingest_audit.json` carries the record by record ledger and the identity work behind it. `/app/out/data_quality.json` carries what the window noticed about its own inputs. `/app/out/slot_designation.json` carries the reserve slots the window held back.

Alongside those, write one report for every domain that is in scope for this window and one for every channel that is in scope, into the same directory, named as the partition rulebook says partition reports are named. The registers this window ships admit eight candidate partition reports, and the naming rule puts them at `/app/out/domain_ledgerworks.json`, `/app/out/domain_meridian.json`, `/app/out/domain_northfield.json`, `/app/out/domain_oakline.json`, `/app/out/domain_penumbra.json`, `/app/out/domain_quarryside.json`, `/app/out/channel_cascade.json` and `/app/out/channel_tidewater.json`. Which of those eight are in scope is a consequence of how the window settles, so the set you write is a result rather than a given, and it is published nowhere. Do not assume it, derive it. Leave every candidate that settles out of scope uncreated: a report that should not exist is as wrong as one that is missing.

This window has two outcomes of equal standing, and it is closed only when both are right. The first is the settled account above. The second is the egress layer the reference set carries in a rulebook filed under E, which reads the curated ledger the settlement produced and settles it onto a per octet basis. It is not an appendix to the settlement and it is not optional: it carries its own six artifacts, its own rules and its own conventions, and a correct settlement with a wrong egress layer is an unclosed window in exactly the way a wrong settlement is. Run it second because it consumes the curated ledger, not because it matters less.

The egress layer turns each curated record into what it cost per octet of payload it carried, holds back the records that burst, and settles the rest into a pool, an apportionment of the window's curated payload units and a digest. Write the egress account to `/app/out/egress_summary.json`, the per-record rates to `/app/out/egress_rates.json`, the records it held back to `/app/out/egress_bursts.json`, the ranked order the digest is taken over to `/app/out/egress_order.json`, the payload apportionment to `/app/out/egress_apportionment.json`, and the per-group rendering to `/app/out/egress_ladder.csv`. The artifact schema fixes the key names, the row shapes and the CSV header of all six; emit the figures under the names it states.

The egress rulebook does not reuse the conventions of the rulebooks above it. Its one division truncates where every other division in the reference set places its result on the settlement grid, its rejection rule names the estimator it uses and the sample size it never rejects from, its medians settle an even sample without averaging and without placing the result, and the order it emits records in is not the canonical ledger order. Its rejection threshold is crossed only by a record that stands strictly above it, so a record sitting exactly on the threshold is retained rather than held back. Take each of those from that rulebook rather than from the ones it sits on top of. Its sigma, its modulus and its octets per payload unit are published in a register of their own.

The artifact the platform produced for the calibration slice is the authority on the form every artifact takes, down to the byte. No prose anywhere describes that form. Match the example.

When you are done, tell me in your final message the charge the window settled, how many records it curated, how many it withdrew and how many it quarantined, the payload units it curated, the feeds it designated as reserve slots, the feeds it quarantined, the domains and channels that ended up in scope, and each of the five recovered properties quoted exactly as you wrote them into the summary. Say what the conservation residuals came to.

Report the egress layer in that same message: the egress pool and the egress digest you settled, the count of curated records the burst rule retained and the count it held back, each record it held back together with the median, the deviation and the threshold that decided it, and the payload share each group took with a confirmation that the shares sum to the curated payload units. Show the per octet arithmetic for one record the rule retained and one it held back.

Everything graded here has to come from what is under `/app/data`. No outside source has this platform or this window in it.

instruction:
The directory `/app/data` holds one backtest extract of Halvard Equipment Finance, which leases equipment to commercial firms and public bodies in four regions. The extract carries the lease book with its branch history, lifecycle events and payment holiday requests, the obligor register with its change events and the public entity register, three payment sources with their returns, two credit bureau feeds with disputes, credit limits, invoice notices, the production snapshot run log, and the champion lease scorecard with its versions, lineage, data incidents and policies. The extract also documents its own layout and rules. Read those documents, work out for yourself what each file holds and which of them actually govern, and reconcile what you find into one contract before you trust any single number.

Backtest the champion out of time: score every lease at every snapshot of the run exactly as it could have been scored at that instant, judge each score against what the lease did afterwards, and report how well the scorecard ranked risk. Every characteristic is the last link of a chain of knowledge-time, identity, schedule, cash, bureau and quarantine decisions, and one wrong link changes plausible numbers with no visible error. Some servicing conventions are never written out: where a document leaves a convention to the evidence, exactly one reading reproduces that evidence, and recovering it from the shipped records is part of the work.

Deliver one reusable program at `/app/out/derive_report.py`, run as `python3 /app/out/derive_report.py DATA_DIR OUT_DIR`, that reads an extract laid out like `/app/data` from DATA_DIR and writes the reports into OUT_DIR. It will also be run on extracts you have not seen, with other leases and obligors, other snapshot dates, steps and counts, other windows, thresholds, tolerances, scorecard versions and incidents, so it must implement the rules and take every parameter from the extract rather than from `/app/data`. Each run, including one on an extract half again as large as `/app/data`, must finish within 300 seconds on one core of this container; a slower run counts as writing nothing. When a required input file is missing, the program must exit with a non zero status and write no report.

Run it on `/app/data` so that its reports land at `/app/out/summary.json`, `/app/out/policy_audit.json`, `/app/out/data_quality.json`, `/app/out/region_North.json`, `/app/out/region_South.json`, `/app/out/region_West.json`, `/app/out/region_East.json`, `/app/out/segment_commercial.json` and `/app/out/segment_public.json`. Those nine files must be exactly what your program writes for `/app/data`. Every report, object, key, value, vocabulary and list order must be exact: a count that is close, a label or reason spelled a shade differently, an entry out of contract order, a float where an integer or null is required, or an invented score or label on an observation that could not be resolved all count as wrong.

The program must use only the Python 3.12 standard library and must install nothing. Its output must depend only on the contents of the input files: the same extract in a directory with another name, or with the lines of its csv and jsonl files in another order, must give the same reports, and two runs must give byte identical files with no timestamps, host names or absolute paths. Write nothing but those nine reports into OUT_DIR, never change DATA_DIR, and leave every file under `/app/data` exactly as shipped. Do not look up solutions online or use hints specific to this task.

When you finish, write a closing message. State the ten what if figures defined under Closing message in `/app/data/output_contract.md`, each as an exact integer labelled with its number and the name of the figure, from runs of your own program with the one stated reading changed. Name every servicing convention the documents leave to the evidence, the reading you settled on for each, and the evidence in the extract that decides it. Give the wall clock time of your program on `/app/data`, and name any report or figure you could not produce.

You have 7200 seconds to complete this task.

instruction:
A source archive at `/app/data/tool.zip` holds a broken offline budget-envelope allocation ledger tool that installs as task-ctl. Extract it to `/app/tool`, repair the tool so it computes correctly, and then use the repaired tool itself to derive a single deterministic allocation-ladder configuration for an offline household budget-envelope ledger. Every rule the configuration must obey is documented across the data files under `/app/data`: how the active allocation band is selected from the base record budget, how the ledger span and its split ratio produce the column width, how per-slot coverage and the effort-per-slot efficiency yield an average allocation, how the ceiling allocation and the reserve envelope follow, how the cycle span and its minimum interval are framed, how the priority step is chosen, and how sharding, rounding buffer, confidence target, helper count, ledger-space bucket/review/ledger class, cadence rate, lookahead, pass count, and temporal layers are set. Those files are densely populated and carry decoy rows; working out which rows are authoritative for the active band, and where the tool's computations diverge from the documented rules, is part of the task.

Repair the tool's faulty numeric and configuration logic in place, and do not bypass, reimplement around, or shadow the tool. The repaired tool has to stay correct for any other rule corpus laid out exactly like `/app/data`, including one it is pointed at through the `TASK_CTL_DATA` environment variable, so every value must come from the corpus the tool reads and never from the shipped numbers; the tool's own command surface is described in the README inside the archive and in the output contract. The data files define the arithmetic policy, the band-selection rule, and the formula for each field; the shipped tool departs from them in several places, and each departure must be found and fixed. Select the active allocation band from the base record budget as documented, and read only the authoritative rows for that band while ignoring every deprecated, phantom, and archived decoy row. Derive the column width, the slot coverage count, the average allocation (clamped to the band's allocation floor and ceiling and quantized to the documented granularity), the ceiling allocation, the reserve envelope, the cycle span, the minimum interval, and the priority step strictly by the documented rules. Set sharding, rounding buffer, confidence target, helpers, ledger-space triple, cadence rate, lookahead, pass count, and temporal layers strictly from the active band's authoritative rows and pinned constants.

Emit the main configuration at `/app/out/config.json` as a single flat JSON object of scalar values only, produced by running the repaired CLI, and validate it through the tool's own validator. Derive the two deployment profiles at `/app/out/profile_dev.json` and `/app/out/profile_prod.json` through the same tool, applying each profile's average-scale, priority, cycle-span, and reserve deltas in the documented order, which applies the scale before granularity. Write the repair-and-run record to `/app/out/report.json` with a truthful command transcript and the configuration digest. Deliver the repaired tool itself as `/app/out/tool.zip`, built deterministically as the output contract describes. Capture the tool's validation output at `/app/out/validation_report.json`, covering every artifact and both profiles. Write a roll-up at `/app/out/summary.json` naming the inputs consumed, the profiles produced, and the artifacts written. The exact field names, object structure, and text layout that each artifact under `/app/out` must use are written out in `/app/data/output_contract.md`, so read that file and follow it exactly for every artifact you emit.

Write the flat solved ladder to `/app/out/ladder_solution.yaml` and the tabular ladder to `/app/out/bitrate_ladder.csv`. Write `/app/out/gop_plan.ini`, `/app/out/vbv_plan.properties`, and `/app/out/qp_curve.psv` describing the cycle-span, reserve, and priority derivations. Write `/app/out/color_config.env`, `/app/out/framerate_plan.kv`, and `/app/out/tiling_plan.toml` for the active band. Write `/app/out/selection_trace.kv` recording the selected band, and `/app/out/rounding_audit.yaml` recording each rounding step. Write `/app/out/profile_delta_report.json` giving the signed main-to-profile deltas, and `/app/out/convergence_report.txt` confirming the derivation is stable across a repeat run. Write `/app/out/reproducibility_manifest.json` pinning the run, `/app/out/derivation_provenance.xml` tracing each derived value to its source file, and `/app/out/input_manifest.ndjson` listing every consumed input. Write `/app/out/ladder_ordering.tsv` listing the main, dev, and prod rungs ordered by ascending average allocation. These artifact and configuration-field names borrow codec-style vocabulary (bitrate, gop, vbv, qp, framerate, tiling, color) purely as an intentional abstract label scheme for this budget-envelope allocation ledger; they carry no video-encoding meaning, and every value is derived solely from the household budget rules documented under `/app/data`.

Use only the Python standard library, and leave nothing under `/app/out` except the 23 artifacts named here. The local files provided under `/app/data` are everything you need; the answer is fully determined by those files and no external host holds any part of it. You have 7200 seconds to complete this task. Do not cheat by pulling an online solution or hints specific to this task.

instruction:
The stable isotope facility published batch HSI-2611, d15N versus AIR and d13C versus VPDB from two EA-IRMS lines, from the saved rerun pack `/app/data/rerun_pack.md`. The published numbers in `/app/data/published_results.csv` and `/app/data/published_session_params.json` are wrong in ways that reach the peak ledger, the tray assignments, every correction stage, the normalization, the session decisions and the sample means. Everything needed to redo the batch from the raw peak exports is under `/app/data`: the handbook `/app/data/method_handbook.md` holds the rules and the order of authority, `/app/data/feed_layouts.md` describes the export layouts, and `/app/data/output_contract.md` fixes the columns, keys, vocabularies, decimals and order of every report. Working out which of the other files can be trusted, and for what, is part of the job.

The finished work is one program, `/app/out/run_irms.py`, run as `python3 /app/out/run_irms.py DATA_DIR OUT_DIR`. It reads a batch laid out like `/app/data` from whatever directory it is given, leaves that directory untouched, and writes into OUT_DIR the twenty-one reports named below plus `/app/out/manifest.json` and nothing else. After your last edit you run it once with `/app/data` as input and `/app/out` as output, so the files left in `/app/out` are its own output. It is run again later on fresh batches placed elsewhere, with other seeds, site clocks, memo tables, profile settings, workbook date systems, journals, rulings and file names, and with memo, workbook and YAML files written by other tools, so every figure has to come out of the input at run time and nothing may be carried over from the shipped files. Each run has to finish within two minutes. Arithmetic and rounding follow the handbook exactly. A report is accepted only when it matches the contract exactly, and every other report rests on the eight core reports (injection ledger, linearity slopes, drift fits, normalization fits, corrected injections, session acceptance, sample results and replicate screening), which have to be exact on the shipped batch and on every fresh batch.

The reports are every kept injection element in `/app/out/injection_ledger.csv`; the tray resolution of every session in `/app/out/position_resolution.csv`; every aliased token in `/app/out/alias_resolution.psv`; the ingest counters in `/app/out/dedup_report.json` and the per-file counts in `/app/out/source_lineage.json`; the linearity slopes and their assignment in `/app/out/linearity_slopes.json`; the drift fits in `/app/out/drift_fits.tsv`; the blank corrections in `/app/out/blank_corrections.psv`; the normalization fits with every screened point in `/app/out/normalization_fits.json`; every corrected injection in `/app/out/corrected_injections.jsonl`; the elemental response factors in `/app/out/elemental_factors.tsv`; the decision for every session and element in `/app/out/session_acceptance.csv`, with each QC check in `/app/out/qc_results.xml`; the sample results in `/app/out/isotope_results.csv`, with the replicate screening in `/app/out/replicate_screening.jsonl`; the governing settings applied in `/app/out/parameters_used.yaml`; the comparisons with the published results in `/app/out/variance_vs_published.csv`, with the published session parameters in `/app/out/session_param_diff.json`, with the QC dashboard in `/app/out/dashboard_disagreements.csv` and with the LIMS cache in `/app/out/cache_divergence.jsonl`; and the summary in `/app/out/reconciliation.md`. The manifest lists the other reports in contract order with their sizes and SHA-256 digests.

Use only the Python standard library and install nothing. Do not modify, add or delete anything under `/app/data`. When you finish, `/app/out` holds only the program and the twenty-two files named above; keep scratch work elsewhere.

Your final message lists the defects of the published run, each with the handbook rule or memo table that overrides it, and names the tables, sheets and files you set aside.

You have 14400 seconds to complete this task. Do not cheat by using online solutions or hints specific to this task.

instruction:
The files in `/app/data` are a mathematical audit extract for a multi-source spectral covariance repair. Produce the final corrected reports required by the local contract, deriving all values from the extract rather than copying visible examples.

Deliver a reusable Python program at `/app/out/reconcile.py`, runnable as `python3 /app/out/reconcile.py DATA_DIR OUT_DIR`. It must write these collected artifacts: `/app/out/global_summary.json`, `/app/out/audit_state.json`, `/app/out/dependency_checks.json`, `/app/out/matrix_all.json`, `/app/out/cohort_Arden.json`, `/app/out/cohort_Beryl.json`, `/app/out/cohort_Canto.json`, `/app/out/cohort_Dorian.json`, `/app/out/source_atlas.json`, `/app/out/source_beacon.json`, `/app/out/source_cygnus.json`, `/app/out/source_draco.json`, `/app/out/variable_hydra.json`, `/app/out/variable_kepler.json`, `/app/out/variable_lyra.json`, `/app/out/variable_orion.json`, `/app/out/variable_pavo.json`, `/app/out/variable_vega.json`, `/app/out/convergence_periods.json`, `/app/out/convergence_constraints.json`, `/app/out/eigen_spectrum.json`, `/app/out/residuals.json`, `/app/out/ledger_effects.json`, `/app/out/reproducibility.json`.

Use `/app/data/schema.md` as the authoritative contract for input meanings, numerical rules, rounding, required JSON keys, and summary definitions. Your program must implement that contract itself, for the shipped extract and for any later extract with the same file format, so do not expect to read the contract again at run time.

Rules you have to work within:

- Treat everything under DATA_DIR as read-only and leave every file there unchanged.
- Write your deliverables only under the OUT_DIR you were given, and read nothing outside DATA_DIR and OUT_DIR.
- Use only the Python standard library, and do not depend on any network service.
- Accept any DATA_DIR and OUT_DIR that match the contract, so the program keeps working on an extract it has not seen. Do not key any behaviour on directory names, find your inputs by the file families the contract lists rather than by fixed file names, and do not hard-code answers taken from the shipped extract.
- Repair the numeric records. The file formats are already sound, so there is nothing to recover there.
- Derive every reported value from the local files, including all linked side tables and audit records. Do not treat a visible example or any single corpus as a lookup table.
- Write JSON deterministically: sorted keys, compact separators, and one trailing newline.
- Keep the integer ppm-style rounded outputs wherever the contract names them, and populate every artifact with the exact keys and summary levels it asks for.

instruction:
You hold the allocation desk of a four-terminal container port named Alpha, Bravo, Charlie and Delta. Twenty-six fortnightly berth allocation cycles, H01 through H26, span 2032. Nominated laytime claims run ahead of the berth-hours the terminals can supply, so each cycle has to be apportioned. Your evidence is the flat corpus in `/app/data`: Notice of Readiness logs, a charter party registry, a legacy fixed-width intake stream, state events, port circulars, approval logs, entitlement ceilings, commitment agreements, capacity declarations, pilotage substitution factors, tide marks, charterer master records and two settlement observation logs. The documents ending in `.md` together with `derivation_policy.ini`, `unit_declarations.ini`, `source_declarations.properties` and `reason_codes.json` are the contract, and the contract is the single source of truth. Read `corpus_index.md` first, since it names every file.

Build `/app/out/apportion_berth.py`. It accepts `--data <dir>` and `--out <dir>`, reads only the corpus handed to it, and writes nine documents: `/app/out/summary.json`, `/app/out/policy_audit.json`, `/app/out/data_quality.json`, `/app/out/terminal_Alpha.json`, `/app/out/terminal_Bravo.json`, `/app/out/terminal_Charlie.json`, `/app/out/terminal_Delta.json`, `/app/out/segment_liner.json` and `/app/out/segment_tramp.json`. Run it over `/app/data` so those nine documents are in place when you stop. Your program will also be run against extracts of this corpus that nobody has seen, at other scales and with other declarations in force, so each rule has to be read from the corpus at run time rather than from a value you noticed once. The Python standard library is all you get and there is no network. Your program raises a Python exception on any missing or unreadable corpus file rather than exiting cleanly, and never launches other processes to do the derivation work.

`output_contract.md` fixes every key, every ordering and every spelling, and `reason_codes.json` fixes the closed vocabularies; both bind to the letter. Each terminal document carries the twenty-six cycles of its berth and one ledger row for each Notice of Readiness that reaches that terminal inside the horizon, ordered by cycle, then by canonical charterer identity, then by reported Notice reference. Every figure is a whole number of berth-hours and exact equality is the bar, so a figure that is merely close is wrong. Canonical identities read like `CHA-0412#2`. Each ledger row carries one outcome and exactly one reason, picked by the precedence that `reason_codes.json` declares. Notices outside the horizon and Notices whose charterer cannot be resolved belong in the out-of-scope list of their terminal document rather than in the ledger, while a Notice that is inside the horizon and cannot claim still keeps its ledger row. `policy_audit.json` records how often each rule fired across the horizon, `data_quality.json` records what each source declared, what parsed and what was admitted, `summary.json` ties the terminals and the segments together, and the two segment documents roll the ledger up by segment.

A reading of a withheld rule that fits only some of its settlement observations is the wrong reading.

Work the evidence in the order the contract sets out, because each later question stands on the earlier answers: which records are admitted at all, then which charterer and epoch each record belongs to, then which records describe one and the same Notice, then which source governs each field, then which circulars and events take effect, then what each Notice may claim, then what each terminal cycle can supply, and only then the allocation itself. Where two rules could both apply to one record the contract says which one wins, so follow it rather than your own habit, and apply each rule no more widely than it is written, since reaching too far costs as much as stopping too short. Treat the corpus as read-only, add nothing to the output directory beyond the nine documents and the program, and make a second run over the same input produce the same bytes.

Close by telling me, in your final message, seven quantities, each of them two exact whole numbers. First, had carried demurrage been ignored entirely, the total granted berth-hours across the horizon and the number of ledger rows whose outcome would change. Second, under the rival reading of the withheld weather-stoppage rule that every settled observation contradicts, the number of Notices whose governing laytime would differ and the resulting total granted berth-hours. Third, with the settled demurrage survival age extended by one cycle, the number of demurrage lots that would expire and the total running demurrage at the end of H26. Fourth, with the clearing rule never applied, the total running demurrage at the end of H26 and the number of ledger rows whose grant would differ. Fifth, the total berth-hours handed out by the indivisible remainder step and the number of terminal cycles where it handed out at least one. Sixth, if the admission instant were lifted for every file, how many of the Notices whose every source row was recorded after it would then claim, and the total they would claim. Seventh, had the port circulars that lack endorsement been applied anyway, the number of Notices whose governing laytime would differ and the number of terminal cycles whose fill level would differ. State each as a plain integer, name the quantity it answers, and say which evidence settled each of the two withheld rules.

You have 10800 seconds to complete this task. Solve it from the corpus in front of you and do not look for solutions, discussions or reference implementations online.

Our backup cluster's snapshot pruner was lost along with its source, and the storage pools are filling up until it is back. Everything left of it is in `/app/data`. `conventions.md` holds the rules the team wrote down, `reports.md` gives the exact shape of the three output files, and `handover.md` holds notes the last on-call engineer wrote from memory. The team does not trust `handover.md`; where it disagrees with `conventions.md` or the worked examples, it is wrong. Read all three notes before you start writing code.

Two worked examples ship with their answers. Their input files carry the prefix `example_a_` or `example_b_`, and the files they should produce carry `example_a_out_` or `example_b_out_`. The four input files with no prefix (`snapshots.jsonl`, `policy.json`, `holds.csv`, `manifest.json`) are the live intake, and nobody has its answers.

`conventions.md` says that six rules of the old pruner were never written down. Working out those six rules from the worked examples is part of the task. They cover which member of a bucket stands for it, the day a week starts on, whether a hold still counts on its `until` date, whether a partial snapshot may stand for a bucket, which copy of a republished id is used, and which clock the buckets and dates are read on.

Both worked examples use mode word zero. The live intake's `manifest.json` carries mode word 254, and the other intakes the program will later meet carry other mode words. `conventions.md` says which seven bit values are in use and that what each bit does was never written down; working out what each bit does is part of the task as well. The live intake has no answers, but its manifest carries a SHA-256 for each report and for each host's kept lines.

Write the pruner as one Python program at `/app/out/prune.py`, run as `python3 /app/out/prune.py IN_DIR OUT_DIR`. It reads the four input files with no prefix from `IN_DIR`, takes the mode word from that folder's `manifest.json`, and writes `keep.json`, `prune.jsonl` and `summary.json` into `OUT_DIR`, byte for byte in the form `reports.md` gives and replacing any copies already there. It exits with status 0 when it has written them. `prune.jsonl` must exist even when it is empty, and the `plan_digest` in `summary.json` must agree with the `keep.json` written in the same run. A run over an intake of a thousand snapshot lines should finish in well under a minute. Write it as named functions, and leave no bare `except` and no debug print in the file.

The same program will later be run on other folders with this layout, with different hosts, volumes, snapshots, policies, holds and damaged lines, so nothing about the shipped folder may be written into the program, including snapshot ids or the plan digest in code or comments. The program must use only the Python 3.12 standard library, must work with no network access, must leave `IN_DIR` unchanged, and must produce identical output when run twice on the same input. Leave everything under `/app/data` as it is.

Run your finished program over `/app/data` into an output directory of your own outside `/app/data`, and then end with a closing report that gives, for the live intake: `snapshots`, `kept`, `pruned`, `held`, `parents`, `retransmitted`, `republished` and the full `plan_digest`, each as your program wrote it, and for each of the seven reason words (`hourly`, `daily`, `weekly`, `monthly`, `hold`, `parent`, `anchor`) the number of live `keep.json` entries that carry it. For each of the six unwritten rules, state the reading you chose and name the worked example file and snapshot id that settled it, or say plainly that the examples did not settle it and you made a choice. For each of the seven mode bits, state what your program does when it is set and name the live manifest digests you compared to settle it, or say that the bit stays open. Also say whether your program reproduced both worked examples byte for byte, and whether its live reports and host digests agree with every digest in the live `manifest.json`.

A partial pruner that is written down and reported on is worth more than a perfect one that never gets finished. Put the program in place and give the closing report within your first hour, and stop any search over rules or bits well before the time limit; a session that is cut off by the limit leaves no answer at all.

instruction:
# Close the pledge docket for window W-2026Q2

You keep the settlement desk for a principal who owes pledges to counterparties.
The quarter is over, and the docket has to be settled, filed and sealed.

Everything the desk holds sits in `/app/data`. Begin at
`/app/data/corpus_index.md`, which names every file in the corpus. The rule
documents beside it carry the charter, the output contract, the call protocol,
source precedence, temporal handling, dependency handling, grace allocation,
reason codes, entity resolution and mode selection. They define every term used
below, and they are the only description of desk practice you get. The
settlement interface and its client live in `/app/service`.

A pledge belongs to the docket when its governing due instant falls inside the
settlement window. A governing due instant comes from the governing record for
that pledge, chosen under source precedence and under the retraction and cutoff
tests the rules state. Origin instants never decide membership.

Resolve every holder reference in the corpus to one holder key. Resolve every due
expression in the business zone of its holder. Expand every recurring commitment
into period instances and apply the period actions that reached the desk in time.
Settle the governing due instant of every pledge, and take the docket from those
instants alone.

Then weigh the evidence. Decide, for each docket pledge, whether discharge
evidence, a waiver grant or nothing governs it. Propagate prerequisite readiness
across the whole dependency graph, including prerequisites that sit outside the
settlement window. Give every docket pledge one final state drawn only from
cleared, tempered_clear, breached, waived, blocked, held and lapsed, plus a
reason code list drawn only from the closed set the rules publish.

Settle the governing mode from the layers the rules name, and run the grace round
only when the governing mode calls for it.

Record the settlement through the interface in `/app/service`. Declare the window
before any other call. Register every docket pledge in dependency order. File a
boundary notice for every pledge that misses the settlement window by less than
the boundary band, so that each exclusion is recorded. Move every pledge through
its events in the order the call protocol requires, on the channel the channel
policy assigns to that event. Record granted minutes. Seal the window, then
confirm the seal.

File these seven artifacts:

`/app/out/report.json`
`/app/out/final_state.json`
`/app/out/transcript_summary.json`
`/app/out/scenario_alpha.json`
`/app/out/scenario_beta.json`
`/app/out/scenario_mode.json`
`/app/out/summary.json`

`/app/data/output_contract.md` fixes the key set, the key spelling, the value
vocabulary, the ordering and the instant form of each one. Emit exactly those
keys and nothing besides. The content of `/app/out/final_state.json` is the
sealed state the interface returns.

Three alternative settlements stand beside the filed one. Alpha repeats the
settlement with no grace round at all. Beta repeats it with every due expression
resolved in the zone the principal occupied at the origin instant of the pledge.
Mode sets both tallies side by side with the authority that settled the governing
mode.

The bar is exact. An artifact counts only when every key, every enum value, every
instant and every minute figure matches. A figure that is close is a figure that
is wrong.

Where sources disagree, the rule documents in `/app/data` govern: the charter
governs docket scope, the output contract governs artifact shape, and the call
protocol governs the interface.

Close with a message to the principal. It has to state, as figures that appear
in none of the artifacts: how many docket pledges took their governing due
instant from a counterparty acknowledgement that beat a surviving register

instruction:
A settlement desk has dumped one fiscal year of its books into `/app/data` and
then lost the program that read them. What survives is the written contract at
`/app/data/schema.md`, the four event files, the reference tables, and the policy
file the desk settled against. Your job is to rebuild the pipeline.

The contract is the authority on every rule: how an event reaches its region,
its currency, its rate and its fiscal period, which events are malformed, how
the per counterparty collateral ladder decides whether an event is accepted at
all, and the exact shape of every figure you must emit. Read it together with
the bytes. Deciding which file feeds which figure is part of the work, so treat
the directory as something to explore rather than a list handed to you.

Deliver a reusable transform program at `/app/out/transform.py`. It takes an
input directory and an output directory and writes every artifact under the
output directory, so the same code settles a directory it has never seen:

```bash
python3 /app/out/transform.py <DATA_DIR> <OUT_DIR>
```

Use only the Python standard library; anything you pip install now will be
absent later. The program must not open network connections or start other
processes. Money is integer USD cents throughout, and every JSON artifact is
written with sorted keys.

Write the normalized event stream to `/app/out/normalized.jsonl`, the book wide
roll-up to `/app/out/summary.json`, the data health report to
`/app/out/data_quality.json`, and the per product roll-up to
`/app/out/product_summary.json`. Write one file per top level region at
`/app/out/region_central.json`, `/app/out/region_east.json`,
`/app/out/region_north.json`, `/app/out/region_south.json` and
`/app/out/region_west.json`, and one file per segment at
`/app/out/segment_consumer.json`, `/app/out/segment_corporate.json`,
`/app/out/segment_enterprise.json` and `/app/out/segment_smb.json`. The keys
inside each file are fixed by the contract. Every region file and every segment
file is written on every run, including a bucket that drew nothing.

Two warnings worth taking seriously. An artifact counts only when every single
value in it is exact, so one cent or one unit out of place costs the whole file.
And the figures interlock: a counterparty's running balance decides which of its
later events are accepted, so an event you settle wrongly moves the balance,
changes which neighbours survive, and shifts every roll-up that touches them.

Finish by posting a closing message that reports what you built, where each
artifact was written, and the nine closing report figures the contract defines.
Those nine appear in no artifact, so they have to come out of your own run.

You have 7200 seconds to complete this task. Do not cheat by using online
solutions or hints specific to this task.
